stem: A team's analytics dashboard sends natural-language queries to a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. CloudWatch shows no throttling, no elevated queue times, and stable, low traffic - yet each individual query still takes longer to answer than the team wants. Someone proposes enabling a cross-Region inference profile to fix the slow responses. Why is this most likely NOT the right fix?
options: Cross-Region inference profiles primarily raise effective throughput and resilience during traffic spikes; they do not shorten the processing time of an individual, already well-provisioned request
Cross-Region inference profiles are only compatible with Provisioned Throughput deployments, not on-demand models
Cross-Region inference profiles require re-architecting the client application before any benefit is realized
Cross-Region inference profiles require switching from the Converse API to the legacy InvokeModel API
explanation: Cross-Region inference profiles add throughput headroom and resilience by routing across Regions during spikes; with no throttling and low, stable traffic, that headroom is not the bottleneck, so per-request latency will not improve. The other options misdescribe the feature - it works with on-demand models, needs no re-architecture, and does not require a different API.

stem: A team is auditing the latency levers available for their Amazon Bedrock workloads. They want to identify which two of the following actually reduce the ACTUAL end-to-end processing time of a single model invocation, as opposed to improving perceived responsiveness, raising throughput/resilience, or reserving capacity. Select TWO.
options: Enabling latency-optimized inference for a supported model
Switching to a smaller, faster model for a narrow task
Enabling response streaming
Enabling a cross-Region inference profile
Purchasing Provisioned Throughput
explanation: Latency-optimized inference serves supported models on faster infrastructure, and a smaller model inherently does less work per request - both cut actual processing time. Streaming only changes when output becomes visible (perceived latency), cross-Region profiles add throughput/resilience during spikes rather than speeding up a single request, and Provisioned Throughput is a capacity/cost lever for steady high-volume traffic.

stem: A platform team is evaluating whether Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference profiles are the right lever for a workload that experiences regional traffic spikes. Which two statements about cross-Region inference profiles are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: They increase effective throughput and resilience by routing requests across multiple AWS Regions during periods of high demand
Applications can adopt them by invoking the profile ID, without re-architecting how requests are submitted
They guarantee a lower response time for any single request compared to invoking the model directly in one Region
They automatically convert on-demand invocations into a Provisioned Throughput deployment
They are required in order to serve any fine-tuned custom model on Bedrock
explanation: Cross-Region inference profiles route requests across Regions to increase effective throughput and resilience, and applications adopt them simply by targeting the profile ID, with no re-architecture required. They do not guarantee a faster single request, do not convert deployments into Provisioned Throughput, and are not a requirement for serving fine-tuned custom models (that requirement generally applies to Provisioned Throughput).

stem: A team wants to use Amazon Bedrock's latency-optimized inference to cut the actual response time of their production workload. During implementation, they discover that the specific model and Region combination they currently use is not among the models Bedrock supports for latency-optimized inference, and the team must keep using this exact model and Region. Which statement BEST reflects the correct next step?
options: Latency-optimized inference only covers a specific set of supported models and Regions; since this combination is unsupported and the model cannot change, the team should pursue a different lever, such as response streaming, for perceived latency
The team should enable latency-optimized inference anyway; Bedrock automatically falls back to standard inference with no functional difference, so there is no need to change anything
A cross-Region inference profile will automatically provide the same actual-latency reduction as latency-optimized inference for any model
The team must purchase Provisioned Throughput, which automatically includes latency-optimized inference for every model it serves
explanation: Latency-optimized inference is limited to specific supported model and Region combinations; when the combination is unsupported and the model cannot change, the team should fall back to a lever like streaming to at least improve perceived latency. The distractors invent behaviors, such as silent fallback, cross-Region profiles duplicating latency-optimized inference, or Provisioned Throughput automatically bundling it, that do not reflect how these Bedrock features actually work.

stem: A team operates a customer-facing Amazon Bedrock chat assistant and must keep using the SAME foundation model. Leadership sets two goals for the next release: (1) users should see the assistant start responding almost immediately, even though full answers take a few seconds to complete, and (2) the assistant must stay available and responsive during unpredictable regional traffic spikes, without redesigning the request-handling code. Which two actions together satisfy BOTH goals? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable response streaming for the chat responses
Invoke the model through a cross-Region inference profile
Switch to a smaller model in the same family
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model
Enable prompt caching for the system prompt
explanation: Streaming satisfies the 'start responding almost immediately' goal by rendering tokens as they arrive, and a cross-Region inference profile satisfies the 'stay resilient during regional spikes without redesign' goal by routing traffic across Regions. Switching models violates the 'same foundation model' constraint, Provisioned Throughput does not by itself deliver multi-Region spike resilience, and prompt caching targets shared static prefixes rather than either stated goal.

stem: A team is comparing two latency levers for an Amazon Bedrock workload: switching to a smaller foundation model versus enabling latency-optimized inference on the current model. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two options?
options: Both options reduce actual latency, but only switching to a smaller model also reduces per-request cost; latency-optimized inference targets latency alone on the existing model
Both options are functionally identical; latency-optimized inference simply renames the smaller-model approach for supported models
Only switching to a smaller model reduces actual latency; latency-optimized inference only improves perceived latency, similar to response streaming
Latency-optimized inference always costs more than Provisioned Throughput, so a smaller model is the only viable cost-saving lever
explanation: Only switching to a smaller model lowers the per-token price and therefore per-request cost; latency-optimized inference keeps the same model and reduces actual latency without compromising accuracy, so it targets latency rather than cost (it can even carry premium pricing). The other options either mischaracterize latency-optimized inference as identical to a smaller model, wrongly demote it to a perceived-latency-only feature like streaming, or make an unsupported cost comparison against Provisioned Throughput.

stem: A team is designing a cost-monitoring-and-control strategy for a growing set of Amazon Bedrock applications. Select the TWO practices that are core, AWS-recommended components of this strategy.
options: Configure CloudWatch alarms on Bedrock invocation metrics such as InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, and Invocations to catch usage spikes early
Configure AWS Budgets to send proactive notifications when actual or forecasted spend approaches a defined threshold
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for every model the application calls, since reserved capacity always lowers total cost
Wait for the monthly AWS invoice and review it after the billing period closes
Increase the model's max-tokens parameter so requests fail less often and need fewer retries
explanation: Usage alarms on Bedrock's CloudWatch metrics and proactive AWS Budgets notifications are the two pillars of cost monitoring and control. Provisioned Throughput only saves money at high, steady, predictable utilization and is a capacity choice, not a monitoring practice; reviewing the invoice after the fact is reactive rather than proactive; and raising max-tokens does not control cost and can increase it.

stem: A Retrieval Augmented Generation assistant on Amazon Bedrock is cost-constrained because CloudWatch shows InputTokenCount is consistently the dominant driver of its bill. Engineer A proposes switching to a foundation model with a much larger context window so more retrieved chunks can be included without truncation. Engineer B proposes adding a reranker and retrieving a smaller, higher-relevance top-k before assembling the prompt. Which engineer's proposal actually addresses the identified cost driver, and why?
options: Engineer B - reducing the number of chunks sent to the model directly cuts input tokens, the identified cost driver
Engineer A - a larger context window is billed at a flat rate regardless of tokens used, so more chunks cost nothing extra
Both proposals reduce cost equally, since context window size and chunk count are unrelated to on-demand token pricing
Neither proposal helps; only purchasing Provisioned Throughput can reduce a RAG workload's cost
explanation: Engineer B's approach reduces the actual number of input tokens sent per request, directly addressing the identified cost driver, while reranking preserves relevance. A larger context window does not change Bedrock's per-token pricing (Engineer A's premise is a common misconception - extra context capacity is not free), and Provisioned Throughput is a capacity/latency choice for steady workloads, not a token-reduction technique.

stem: An AWS Budgets alert fires because this month's Amazon Bedrock spend already exceeds 90 percent of the planned amount with several days left in the billing cycle. To determine whether the overage is being driven by more requests or by larger requests, which comparison should the team make first?
options: Compare the trend of the Invocations metric against the trend of InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount over the same period
Compare the trend of InvocationLatency against the AWS Budgets forecasted total
Review only the final forecasted dollar amount reported by AWS Budgets
Purchase Provisioned Throughput immediately to cap the bill
explanation: Invocations isolates request volume while InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount isolate request size, so comparing their trends separates a volume-driven overage from a size-driven one. InvocationLatency does not indicate cost, the forecasted dollar total is the symptom under investigation rather than a diagnostic, and buying Provisioned Throughput changes the billing model without first identifying the root cause.

stem: A Retrieval Augmented Generation application on Amazon Bedrock has grown expensive, and a cost dashboard built on CloudWatch metrics shows InputTokenCount is by far the largest contributor to billed tokens. The team wants to both reduce this cost driver going forward and keep watching for regressions. Which two actions should they take? (Select TWO.)
options: Add a reranker and reduce the number of retrieved chunks (top-k) sent to the model so fewer, more relevant chunks are included in the prompt
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InputTokenCount metric so future increases in retrieved-context size are caught early
Increase the number of chunks retrieved per query to raise the chance the answer is present somewhere in the context
Disable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging so fewer resources are consumed per request
Purchase Provisioned Throughput sized for peak traffic to reduce the per-token price of every request
explanation: Reranking a sufficiently broad candidate set and sending fewer relevant chunks to generation can reduce input tokens. A CloudWatch alarm on InputTokenCount helps detect subsequent input-volume increases. Use Average or per-request analysis when diagnosing prompt-size changes, because Sum can also rise with more calls. More context increases tokens; disabling logs does not shrink the prompt; provisioned capacity does not remove redundant context.

stem: To cut Amazon Bedrock cost, a team simply lowers the number of chunks retrieved per query (top-k) for their RAG application, without changing any other part of the retrieval pipeline. Afterward, InputTokenCount drops as expected, but answer quality noticeably degrades because relevant chunks are now sometimes excluded. Which change would let the team keep the lower InputTokenCount while restoring answer quality?
options: Revert top-k to its original, higher value
Add a reranker so the highest-relevance chunks are prioritized within the smaller retrieved set
Switch to a larger, more capable generation model to compensate for the missing context
Increase the chunk size so each retrieved chunk carries more surrounding text
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0661 for current practice. A reranker scores and reorders only the documents supplied to it. Keeping broad candidate retrieval preserves the opportunity to select relevant passages, while limiting the final reranked result count controls generation context. Reranking an already reduced set cannot recover excluded documents. Evaluate retrieval quality and include reranker charges when comparing total cost.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Separates candidate retrieval from final generation context and removes the claim that a reranker recovers unseen chunks.

stem: Two weeks after a marketing campaign launch, finance flags that the Amazon Bedrock bill has roughly tripled. The team's CloudWatch dashboard shows the Invocations metric up about three-fold for the period, while the Average statistic for InputTokenCount and for OutputTokenCount are essentially unchanged from before the campaign. Which conclusion and follow-up action are best supported by these metrics?
options: The cost increase is driven by prompt bloat, so the team should shorten the system prompt and enable prompt caching

The cost increase is driven by higher request volume from more users, so the team should treat this as a capacity-planning signal and keep monitoring whether the higher volume is sustained before making further cost or infrastructure decisions
The cost increase is driven by a change in the underlying foundation model, so the team should pin the model version
The cost increase is driven by slower responses causing retries, so the team should investigate InvocationLatency first
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0662 for current practice. Tripled Invocations with unchanged average input and output token counts supports a request-volume explanation, assuming the model, rates and other billed features are unchanged. These metrics do not prove more distinct users or rule out retries; use request logs if that distinction matters. Monitor whether the volume persists before making capacity commitments. Larger prompts would increase average input tokens, and no model-change or latency evidence is supplied.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Uses the actual metric source and avoids treating request counts as proof of distinct users or excluding retries without evidence. Replaces the unsupported option inference that accepted calls prove more distinct users.

stem: A media company operates a general-purpose creative-writing assistant on Amazon Bedrock that handles unpredictable requests spanning poetry, brainstorming, code snippets, and open-ended Q&A, all served by one large frontier model. Inference cost is high, so someone proposes distilling the frontier model into a smaller student model to cut cost. What is the strongest concern with this proposal?
options: Distillation works best for a narrow, well-defined task; a broad assistant spanning many unrelated skills is a poor fit because a smaller student is unlikely to retain the teacher's full breadth of capability.
Distillation cannot reduce cost unless the workload is first moved to Bedrock batch inference.
Distillation requires the workload to already be running on Provisioned Throughput before a student model can even be trained.
Distillation is purely a latency optimization and has no effect on per-request inference cost.
explanation: Distillation is aimed at a narrow, high-volume task; a broad, multi-skill assistant risks losing quality across the skills the smaller student was not specifically trained to replicate. The other options misstate distillation's mechanics: it is not tied to batch inference, does not require Provisioned Throughput as a precondition for training, and its primary benefit for this domain is exactly cost reduction.

stem: After distilling a frontier teacher model into a smaller student model on Amazon Bedrock for a high-volume email-routing task, a team wants to confirm the student's accuracy is acceptable before shifting all production traffic away from the teacher model. Which practice BEST supports that decision?
options: Retire the teacher model immediately and monitor the student's CloudWatch InvocationLatency metric to confirm output quality.
Run a model evaluation comparing the student and teacher on a representative, held-out set of prompts before cutting traffic over.
Raise the student model's temperature so its outputs more closely resemble the teacher's.
Skip a formal evaluation, since a distilled student model always matches teacher accuracy on the task it was trained for.
explanation: A model evaluation on a held-out, representative prompt set is the way to confirm the student retains acceptable accuracy before it takes over production traffic. InvocationLatency measures speed, not answer quality; temperature controls output randomness, not fidelity to the teacher; and distillation provides no guarantee of matching teacher accuracy, so skipping evaluation is unsafe.

stem: A logistics company is deciding whether Amazon Bedrock model distillation is worth the up-front training effort for a narrow, very high-volume text-classification workload currently served by a frontier model. Select TWO statements that correctly describe what distillation delivers for this pattern.
options: A smaller student model produced through distillation typically lowers the per-token inference cost compared with continuing to run the frontier teacher model.
Because the student model is smaller, it commonly also improves inference latency relative to the larger teacher model.
The distilled student model is guaranteed to produce outputs identical to the teacher model on every input.
Once distilled, the student model can always be served on-demand regardless of its model family, eliminating any need to ever provision Provisioned Throughput.
Distillation removes the need to evaluate the student model's accuracy before it is used in production.
explanation: Distillation's core value for a narrow, high-volume task is a smaller, cheaper student model that also tends to respond faster than the large teacher. It provides no guarantee of identical outputs, does not universally unlock on-demand serving (most custom models still need Provisioned Throughput), and does not remove the need to evaluate the student before production cutover.

stem: A team plans to use Amazon Bedrock model distillation to cut the cost of a narrow, high-volume invoice line-item classification task that is currently served by a frontier teacher model already meeting accuracy targets. Which TWO statements correctly describe how the team should apply model distillation in this case? (Select TWO)
options: Use the frontier teacher model to produce or curate task-specific example outputs, then use those outputs to train a smaller student model so it captures the teacher's behavior for this task.
Distillation is best applied to broad, open-ended conversational workloads rather than narrow, well-defined tasks.
Serve the resulting student model via Provisioned Throughput, or on-demand if the student's model family supports on-demand deployment of custom models.
Skip evaluating the student model's accuracy, since distillation automatically matches teacher-level accuracy.
Distillation eliminates the need to ever purchase Provisioned Throughput for any custom model on Bedrock.
explanation: Distillation works by training a smaller student model on the teacher's task-specific outputs, and the resulting student is then served via Provisioned Throughput or on-demand where its model family supports on-demand custom-model deployment. It targets narrow, high-volume tasks (not broad conversational workloads), the student's accuracy still must be evaluated rather than assumed, and Provisioned Throughput remains required for most custom models regardless of distillation.

stem: A team has a small labeled dataset of correctly triaged support tickets and is choosing between two options for a narrow, high-volume triage task currently run at high cost on a frontier model that meets accuracy on Amazon Bedrock. Option A fine-tunes a small foundation model directly on the small labeled dataset. Option B uses model distillation: the frontier model generates labels across a much larger set of representative tickets, and those labels train the small student model. Which factor is the strongest reason to prefer Option B for preserving the frontier model's accuracy characteristics on this task?
options: Option B trains the smaller model against the teacher's own outputs across a broader set of examples, transferring the frontier model's task-specific behavior more directly than fine-tuning on the small original dataset alone.
Option B is guaranteed to cost less per month than Option A, regardless of training data volume.
Option B never requires Provisioned Throughput to serve the resulting model.
Option B removes the need to evaluate the student model against a held-out set before production use.
explanation: Distillation's core value is that the student model learns from the teacher's own outputs over a broad example set, more directly reproducing the frontier model's task-specific behavior than fine-tuning on a small hand-labeled dataset. The other options misstate guarantees about cost, serving requirements, or the ongoing need to evaluate the student model.

stem: A retail shopping assistant on Amazon Bedrock opens every request with the same 3,500-token product-catalog summary and shipping-policy excerpt, then appends a different shopper question each time. The team wants to lower cost and speed up the first token of the response for the repeated portion. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Enable prompt caching and place a cache checkpoint immediately after the catalog summary and shipping-policy excerpt
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model to guarantee dedicated capacity
Submit the requests through Bedrock batch inference instead of synchronous invocation
Distill the model's behavior into a smaller custom model
explanation: Prompt caching is the go-to technique when the same large static prefix is sent on every request; caching it cuts cost on cache hits and reduces time-to-first-token. Provisioned Throughput addresses steady high-utilization capacity, not repeated-prefix cost; batch inference is asynchronous and unsuitable for a live shopper-facing assistant; distillation trades a smaller model for lower cost/latency but does not target the repeated-prefix problem directly.
exclusionReason: Unresolved after source review: Generic model-free prompt-caching questions use prefixes below 4096 tokens. Some supported Claude models require4096, while others require512 or1024.

stem: A team enables Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for a workload where every request shares a common instruction prefix. Which statement correctly describes what happens on a cache hit?
options: Tokens within the cached prefix are billed at a reduced rate, and time-to-first-token typically drops because the prefix is not reprocessed
Output tokens are billed at a reduced rate, and the model's maximum context window increases
The request is automatically routed to Provisioned Throughput capacity at no extra charge
The model skips generating a response entirely for prefixes it has seen before
explanation: On a cache hit, cached input tokens are billed at a large discount and time-to-first-token improves because the static prefix does not need to be reprocessed. It does not discount output tokens, does not change the context window, does not route to Provisioned Throughput, and it does not skip generating a response.

stem: A voice-enabled customer service bot on Amazon Bedrock opens every turn with the same block of system instructions and tool definitions, then appends a conversation transcript that keeps growing turn after turn plus the newest caller utterance. The team enables prompt caching to reduce cost as the session continues. Where should the cache checkpoint be placed so the static block is served from cache on every turn?
options: Immediately after the fixed system instructions and tool definitions, before the growing conversation transcript
At the very beginning of the request, before the system instructions
At the very end of the request, after the newest caller utterance
No checkpoint is needed; Bedrock caches the entire prompt automatically regardless of content
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0663 for current practice. For explicit caching, placing a checkpoint after the stable instructions and tool definitions clearly marks the prefix the team wants to reuse while later content changes. Eligibility, minimums and TTL still apply, and reads are not guaranteed on every turn. Supported models can also provide implicit caching without checkpoints, and model-specific block lookback may reuse earlier content from a later checkpoint. The selected placement is a clear explicit boundary rather than the only possible caching path.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Retains sensible explicit checkpoint placement but acknowledges implicit caching and model-specific lookback.

stem: A legal research tool on Amazon Bedrock lets a user ask several follow-up questions about the same 12,000-token contract within one session. Each request resends the full contract text along with the new question. Which change would MOST directly reduce the cost of resending the contract text on each follow-up?
options: Enable prompt caching with a checkpoint placed after the contract text
Increase the model's temperature to shorten generated responses
Switch the workload to Bedrock batch inference
Enable response streaming for the follow-up answers
explanation: Since the large contract text repeats verbatim across follow-up requests in the same session, caching it after a checkpoint lets subsequent requests reuse the cached tokens at a discount instead of paying full price to resend it. Temperature affects output randomness, not the cost of repeated input; batch inference is for asynchronous bulk jobs, not an interactive follow-up session; streaming improves perceived latency but does not reduce token cost.

stem: A multi-tenant SaaS platform built on Amazon Bedrock lets each customer configure its own large custom system prompt. Every request from a given tenant reuses that tenant's own system prompt unchanged, but the prompt differs from one tenant to the next. Does enabling prompt caching still help reduce cost for this platform?
options: Yes, because caching operates per distinct prefix; each tenant's repeated system prompt can be cached independently and benefit that tenant's own requests
No, because prompt caching only produces a cache hit when the exact same prefix is shared across every tenant on the platform
No, because prompt caching requires all requests platform-wide to be sent within the same second
Yes, but only after the tenants are consolidated onto a single shared system prompt
explanation: A cache hit occurs whenever a request repeats a previously cached prefix, and that comparison happens per distinct prefix, not across the whole platform, so each tenant's own repeated system prompt is independently cacheable and benefits that tenant's subsequent requests. Caching does not require every tenant to share identical text, does not require simultaneous requests, and does not require consolidating tenants onto one prompt.

stem: A content-moderation classifier on Amazon Bedrock includes a fixed 2,500-token taxonomy of violation categories and definitions at the start of every request, followed by a single short message to classify. The classifier is invoked several thousand times per hour. Which approach is MOST appropriate to lower cost without changing the classification logic?
options: Enable prompt caching with a checkpoint placed after the taxonomy block
Move the workload to Bedrock batch inference so requests are processed asynchronously
Enable cross-Region inference profiles to spread the requests across Regions
Enable latency-optimized inference for the classifier's model
explanation: The fixed taxonomy block repeats on every one of the many requests, which is exactly the pattern prompt caching targets: cache it once and reuse it at a discount on subsequent calls. Batch inference would break the near-real-time classification flow; cross-Region inference profiles address throughput and resilience, not repeated-prefix cost; latency-optimized inference improves actual inference speed but does not discount repeated input tokens.
exclusionReason: Unresolved after source review: Generic model-free prompt-caching questions use prefixes below 4096 tokens. Some supported Claude models require4096, while others require512 or1024.

stem: A company builds an internal coding assistant integrated into an IDE. Every code-completion request sends the same 8,000-token engineering style guide and repository coding conventions ahead of the unique code snippet the developer is working on. The team wants to lower per-request cost and reduce time-to-first-token without changing the underlying model. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model to guarantee dedicated capacity.
Move the workload to Amazon Bedrock batch inference to process requests asynchronously.
Enable prompt caching on the model and place a cache checkpoint immediately after the shared style guide and coding conventions.
Reduce the max_tokens parameter on each request to shorten model output.
explanation: Enabling prompt caching with a checkpoint after the large shared prefix (the style guide and conventions) lets Bedrock reuse the already-processed tokens on every subsequent call, cutting cost and time-to-first-token. Provisioned Throughput addresses steady high-volume capacity, not repeated-prefix cost; batch inference is for asynchronous bulk jobs, not an interactive IDE assistant; reducing max_tokens only affects output length, not the cost of resending the static input.

stem: A team is about to implement prompt caching for a new Bedrock application that sends a shared 2,000-token onboarding script ahead of every user turn. Before rolling it out, an engineer wants to confirm exactly what enabling prompt caching changes. Which statement is correct?
options: Enabling prompt caching automatically provisions dedicated Provisioned Throughput capacity for the workload.
Input tokens that match a previously cached prefix are billed at a reduced rate, and time-to-first-token drops because that prefix does not need to be reprocessed.
Output tokens generated by the model are billed at a reduced rate once caching is enabled.
The model is fine-tuned on the cached onboarding script so it no longer needs to be sent on future requests.
explanation: Prompt caching discounts the cached (repeated) input tokens and reduces time-to-first-token because Bedrock does not need to reprocess the static prefix. It has no effect on output token pricing, does not fine-tune or otherwise train the model, and is unrelated to Provisioned Throughput routing.
exclusionReason: Unresolved after source review: Generic model-free prompt-caching questions use prefixes below 4096 tokens. Some supported Claude models require4096, while others require512 or1024.

stem: A multi-turn conversational assistant on Amazon Bedrock resends the entire growing conversation history with every new user turn so the model retains context. As conversations get longer, latency and cost per turn increase noticeably. Which change would MOST directly address this?
options: Switch the workload from on-demand to Provisioned Throughput.
Submit each turn as a separate Amazon Bedrock batch inference job.
Enable response streaming so tokens render as they are generated.
Enable prompt caching and extend the cache checkpoint to cover the conversation history that was already sent in prior turns.
explanation: Extending the prompt-cache checkpoint to cover the already-sent conversation history lets Bedrock reuse those previously processed tokens instead of reprocessing the whole transcript each turn, cutting both cost and time-to-first-token. Provisioned Throughput and batch inference do not address repeated-prefix reprocessing, and streaming only improves perceived latency of the output, not the cost or delay caused by reprocessing history.

stem: An orchestrator agent built on Amazon Bedrock calls the same foundation model dozens of times per user request, once per sub-task. Every call includes an identical 6,000-token block describing the available tools and their schemas, followed by a short, unique instruction for that sub-task. Which change reduces cost and latency with the least architectural disruption?
options: Split the tool-definition block across multiple smaller foundation models.
Enable prompt caching with a checkpoint placed after the shared tool-definition block, before the unique per-call instruction.
Move the orchestrator workload to batch inference so all sub-task calls run as one job.
Distill the tool-definition reasoning into a smaller student model.
explanation: Placing a cache checkpoint right after the shared, unchanging tool-definition block lets every sub-task call reuse the cached tokens for that prefix, since it is identical each time, while the varying instruction after the checkpoint is processed normally. Splitting definitions across models adds complexity without addressing repeated processing, batch inference breaks the orchestrator's interactive sub-task calls, and distillation targets accuracy-for-cost tradeoffs on a narrow task, not repeated-prefix reprocessing.

stem: An internal-wiki question-answering assistant on Amazon Bedrock sends the same 10,000-token reference article in full ahead of every question a user asks during a session, since the team wants the model to see the complete article each time rather than a retrieved excerpt. Which change would MOST reduce cost and response latency while keeping the full article visible to the model on every call?
options: Fine-tune the model on the reference article so it no longer needs to be sent.
Increase the top-k value used during retrieval so more of the article is included.
Enable prompt caching with a checkpoint placed immediately after the reference article.
Switch the workload to Amazon Bedrock batch inference.
explanation: Caching the reference article as a shared prefix means Bedrock only processes it once and reuses it at a discount for every subsequent question in the session, lowering cost and time-to-first-token while still sending the full article. Fine-tuning does not reliably embed exact reference text and adds cost/complexity; increasing top-k would add more tokens, not fewer; batch inference is unsuitable for an interactive session.

stem: A team enables prompt caching for a support assistant, but structures each request with the unique customer question FIRST, followed by the large static company policy text, and places the cache checkpoint at the very end of the prompt. They observe little to no reduction in cost or time-to-first-token. What is the MOST likely cause, and how should it be fixed?
options: The model being used does not support prompt caching, so the team must switch to a Provisioned Throughput model unit.
The cache checkpoint should be removed entirely, since caching only works with batch inference jobs.
The static policy text is too large to be cached and must be shortened below the model's context window before caching will take effect.
Prompt caching only benefits an identical shared prefix; the static policy text must be moved to the beginning of the prompt with the checkpoint placed right after it, ahead of the unique question.
explanation: Caching only reuses tokens that form an identical prefix across requests; because the unique question comes first, no two requests share the same leading tokens, so nothing is cached. Moving the static, repeated policy text to the front and placing the checkpoint right after it restores the benefit. Model support and context-window size are not the described problem, and caching is unrelated to batch inference.

stem: A high-volume customer-support bot on Amazon Bedrock already uses prompt caching for its 5,000-token static system instructions. Despite this, the team's monthly bill is still dominated by input token costs, because each request also includes a unique customer question and a large block of freshly retrieved knowledge-base content that differs every time. Which statement correctly explains why prompt caching alone has not reduced this remaining cost?
options: Prompt caching was configured incorrectly; if configured correctly, it would also discount unique, non-repeating tokens.
Prompt caching only applies to output tokens, so it was never going to affect the input token costs described here.

Prompt caching only discounts tokens that are part of a repeated, identical prefix; the unique question and freshly retrieved content differ on every call, so those tokens are always processed and billed at standard rates regardless of caching.
The retrieved knowledge-base content must be moved before the cache checkpoint so caching can discount it as well.
explanation: Prompt caching discounts only the portion of the prompt that is an identical, repeated prefix across requests; the per-request question and freshly retrieved content are different every time by design, so they can never be cached and continue to be billed as standard input tokens - the team would need a different lever (for example tighter retrieval/reranking or a smaller model) to reduce that portion. This is not a configuration error, caching affects input (not output) tokens, and moving unique content before the checkpoint would not make it cacheable since it still would not match across calls.

stem: A brand-new mobile app is about to launch with no historical traffic data. Usage on launch day could range from a few dozen requests to tens of thousands, and the team has no budget for a term commitment. Which Amazon Bedrock inference option is MOST appropriate for invoking the foundation model?
options: On-demand inference, paying per token with no capacity commitment
Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment term
Batch inference submitted once per day
Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month commitment term
explanation: On-demand is the default pay-per-token mode built for variable or unpredictable traffic with no upfront commitment, which fits an unknown launch-day pattern. Both Provisioned Throughput options lock the team into a term commitment that only pays off with high, steady utilization, and batch inference is asynchronous and unsuitable for a live app.

stem: A developer proposes routing every request from a live, interactive customer-support chat widget through Amazon Bedrock batch inference to cut costs. Why is this MOST likely the wrong choice?
options: Batch inference is an asynchronous, bulk-processing mode and cannot deliver the near-real-time responses an interactive chat requires
Batch inference only supports embedding models, not text-generation models
Batch inference charges a higher per-token rate than on-demand inference
Batch inference requires the underlying model to be fine-tuned first
explanation: Batch inference runs prompts as asynchronous bulk jobs at discounted pricing and is never the right choice for an interactive experience because it does not return a response synchronously. It supports many model types beyond embeddings, typically costs less rather than more, and has no fine-tuning prerequisite.

stem: A compliance department needs roughly 40,000 contracts signed over the past three years translated into a second language once, as part of a quarterly archival review. The results are not needed for several days. Which approach minimizes cost while meeting this requirement?
options: Submit the documents as an asynchronous batch inference job at discounted pricing
Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month term to guarantee capacity
Invoke the model on-demand with maximum parallel requests to finish quickly
Enable prompt caching on the document invocations to lower cost
explanation: A large, one-time job with no real-time deadline is the textbook case for batch inference, which processes bulk requests asynchronously at a discount. Provisioned Throughput is meant for steady, high-utilization traffic rather than a one-off quarterly job, brute-force on-demand concurrency costs more per token than batch, and prompt caching only helps when the same static prefix repeats across requests, not unique per-document content.

stem: A team fine-tunes an Amazon Nova model using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to specialize it for support-ticket triage, and expects modest, fluctuating traffic. The team wants to avoid committing to Provisioned Throughput if at all possible. What should they do?
options: Deploy the custom Nova PEFT model for on-demand inference, since this model family is a documented exception to the general custom-model requirement
Purchase Provisioned Throughput anyway, since every custom model on Bedrock requires it with no exceptions
Route every triage request through batch inference instead of serving it interactively
There is no way to avoid a throughput commitment; fine-tuned models can only run on the largest available Provisioned Throughput tier
explanation: Amazon Nova PEFT fine-tunes (along with Meta Llama 3.3 70B customs) are a documented exception that can be served with on-demand inference, unlike most custom models. Claiming there are 'no exceptions' is wrong given this carve-out, batch inference does not fit interactive triage traffic, and no model is locked into only the largest Provisioned Throughput tier.

stem: A downstream fraud-review workflow needs classification results for a batch of 5,000 transaction records within a fixed 10-minute window, after which the results are discarded as stale. Which inference mode should the team choose?
options: Batch inference, because any bulk dataset belongs in an asynchronous batch job
On-demand inference, invoked with enough concurrency to comfortably finish inside the deadline
Provisioned Throughput with a term commitment sized only for this one job
Batch inference, split across several smaller batch jobs to shorten completion time
explanation: Batch inference is asynchronous and does not guarantee a completion time, so it is unsuitable whenever there is a strict fixed deadline, even for a moderately large dataset; on-demand inference invoked with adequate concurrency is what can reliably meet a hard time window. Splitting work across several batch jobs does not turn batch into a low-latency, deadline-bound mode, and a term-based Provisioned Throughput commitment is the wrong tool for a single one-off job.

stem: A back-office reporting tool calls a Bedrock model exactly 200 times per hour, every hour, with almost no variation day to day - a highly steady and predictable pattern. However, 200 requests per hour is a small volume compared to the platform's larger customers. A team member argues that this steady, predictable pattern alone means Provisioned Throughput should be purchased. Is this reasoning sound?
options: No - Provisioned Throughput is cost-effective only when utilization is high AND steady AND predictable together, and low volume can still leave reserved capacity underutilized relative to its cost
Yes - steadiness and predictability are the only two factors that matter when choosing Provisioned Throughput
No - Provisioned Throughput can never be purchased for a low-volume workload under any circumstances
Yes - Provisioned Throughput bills per token just like on-demand, so volume does not affect the comparison
explanation: Provisioned Throughput only becomes cheaper than on-demand when utilization is high, steady, and predictable together; steady but low volume can still leave reserved model units underused relative to their fixed hourly/term cost. Steadiness and predictability alone are not sufficient, there is no absolute rule banning low-volume workloads from Provisioned Throughput, and it bills for reserved capacity at a fixed rate rather than per token, so volume does affect the comparison.

stem: An internal tool must call a Bedrock model and receive the generated answer within the same HTTP request/response cycle, with no polling or callback involved, so the calling service can use the result immediately. Traffic is steady but modest, and the team has no interest in a capacity commitment. Which inference option fits this requirement?
options: On-demand inference
Batch inference
Provisioned Throughput
Asynchronous batch inference with short-polling for results
explanation: On-demand returns results synchronously within the same call, matching a workload that needs no polling and no term commitment. Batch inference, with or without polling, is asynchronous by design and cannot return an answer within the same request/response cycle, and Provisioned Throughput requires a capacity commitment the team wants to avoid.

stem: A newly launched mobile app has unknown and highly variable request volume during its first month in production, and the team wants to avoid any upfront capacity commitment while it gathers real usage data. Which throughput mode should the team use to invoke the Amazon Bedrock foundation model?
options: On-demand inference
Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month commitment
Batch inference
Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment
explanation: On-demand requires no capacity commitment and is the right default for variable or unpredictable traffic. Both Provisioned Throughput options assume steady, high utilization the team has no data to justify yet, and batch inference is asynchronous, not suited to a live app.

stem: A retail analytics team regenerates rewritten product descriptions for 2 million catalog items once per week. The output feeds a downstream search-indexing job hours later, and no user is waiting on any individual result. Which throughput mode minimizes cost for this workload?
options: On-demand inference invoked in a tight loop over all 2 million items
Batch inference
Provisioned Throughput sized for the weekly peak volume
On-demand inference behind an Amazon SQS queue for backpressure
explanation: Batch inference is built for large, asynchronous jobs like this and bills at discounted rates. Provisioned Throughput only pays off with steady, high utilization, which a once-a-week burst does not provide, and queuing on-demand calls still pays full on-demand per-token rates.

stem: A team fine-tuned an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock and now needs to put it into production for a customer-facing feature. Which throughput mode(s) can serve this custom model?
options: On-demand inference only
Provisioned Throughput only
Batch inference only
Either on-demand or Provisioned Throughput, at the team's discretion
explanation: Most custom (fine-tuned) models on Bedrock require Provisioned Throughput to serve inference, and Claude fine-tunes are not among the on-demand exceptions (which currently cover only Amazon Nova PEFT fine-tunes and Meta Llama 3.3 70B custom models). Batch inference and unrestricted on-demand access are not available for this model.

stem: A team fine-tuned Meta Llama 3.3 70B on Amazon Bedrock for an internal tool with low, sporadic usage, and wants to avoid paying for reserved capacity between invocations. Which deployment option is available to this specific custom model that is NOT available to most other custom (fine-tuned) models on Bedrock?
options: Batch inference for every invocation, including single ad hoc requests
On-demand inference
A Provisioned Throughput commitment with no minimum term
Deployment outside of Amazon Bedrock entirely
explanation: Meta Llama 3.3 70B Instruct is listed for custom-model on-demand deployment in US West (Oregon), subject to the customization-date and deployment prerequisites. Invoke the active deployment ARN rather than assuming a raw custom-model ID is an on-demand endpoint. This avoids paying for reserved capacity between calls. Provisioned Throughput also has no-commitment options for supported models, but those still charge for provisioned capacity while allocated.

stem: To cut costs, an engineering lead proposes rerouting all live customer-chat messages through Batch inference, reasoning that batch pricing is cheaper per token than on-demand. What is the primary problem with this plan?
options: Batch inference cannot access foundation models that support conversational prompts.
Batch inference is asynchronous and does not guarantee the near-real-time responses a live chat interface requires.
Batch inference requires purchasing Provisioned Throughput model units before it can be used.
Batch inference can only process structured data, not natural language text.
explanation: Batch inference is an asynchronous, bulk mechanism with no real-time response guarantee, so it is never the right fit for an interactive chat experience regardless of its per-token discount. The other options misstate what batch inference actually requires and supports.

stem: A developer calls the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API directly against a base foundation model's model ID, without referencing any Provisioned Throughput ARN and without submitting a batch job. Which throughput mode processes this request?
options: On-demand inference
Provisioned Throughput
Batch inference
The request fails until a throughput mode is explicitly selected
explanation: Calling the base model ID directly, with no Provisioned Throughput ARN and no batch job, invokes the model in on-demand mode, Bedrock's default pay-per-token path. Provisioned Throughput requires referencing a provisioned model ARN, and batch inference requires submitting a separate asynchronous job; neither happens implicitly.

stem: A FinOps lead wants next month's Bedrock bill for a specific high-volume, fairly steady production workload to be a fixed, predictable amount regardless of small day-to-day swings in call volume, even if the workload sometimes runs a bit below capacity. Which throughput mode best supports this goal?
options: On-demand inference, since its per-token pricing scales precisely with actual usage
Provisioned Throughput, since it reserves capacity at a fixed hourly or term rate independent of exact call volume
Batch inference, since discounted job pricing is inherently more predictable
A mix of on-demand and batch inference, alternated daily
explanation: Provisioned Throughput bills at a fixed rate for reserved model units regardless of exact daily call volume within capacity, giving predictable bills for a steady workload. On-demand and batch pricing both scale with actual token or job volume, so they vary with usage rather than staying fixed.

stem: An internal HR policy Q&A tool on Amazon Bedrock has an average InvocationLatency that is stable and within the team's SLA. Even so, employees frequently click Send a second time, assuming their first request failed, because nothing appears in the chat pane for several seconds while the model finishes the full answer. The team wants to stop the duplicate submissions without changing how long the model actually takes to generate an answer. Which change is MOST appropriate?
options: Enable response streaming so partial output appears as tokens are generated
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model
Move the workload to batch inference
Enable a cross-Region inference profile
explanation: Response streaming renders tokens as they are produced, so employees see progress immediately even though total generation time (InvocationLatency) is unchanged, which stops the duplicate-submission behavior. Provisioned Throughput and cross-Region profiles are capacity/throughput levers unrelated to when output first appears, and batch inference is asynchronous and unsuitable for an interactive Q&A tool.

stem: A mobile messaging app calls a large, general-purpose foundation model on Amazon Bedrock to generate three short quick-reply suggestions while the user is actively typing. The suggestions are simple and short, but they consistently arrive too late to be useful before the user finishes typing. Monthly Bedrock spend is well within budget and is not a concern. Which change is MOST likely to make the suggestions appear fast enough to be useful?
options: Switch the quick-reply feature to a smaller, faster model sized for lightweight tasks (e.g., Amazon Nova Micro)
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the current large model
Move the quick-reply calls to Amazon Bedrock batch inference
Enable prompt caching for the request
explanation: For a narrow, low-complexity task, swapping to a smaller, faster foundation model cuts actual generation latency (and cost) far more than reserving capacity for the same large model. Provisioned Throughput improves availability/cost at high steady utilization but does not shrink the large model's own generation time; batch inference is asynchronous and unusable for as-you-type suggestions; prompt caching only helps when a large static prefix repeats, which is not described here.

stem: An internal legal-research assistant on Amazon Bedrock is being investigated for latency complaints. CloudWatch shows InvocationLatency (time for the full response) is essentially unchanged from before, but attorneys still describe replies as sluggish. The team wants to specifically shorten the delay before any visible output appears, without changing the model or its configuration. Which capability directly targets this gap?
options: ConverseStream / InvokeModelWithResponseStream to stream the response as tokens are produced
Latency-optimized inference
A cross-Region inference profile
Provisioned Throughput
explanation: Streaming APIs (ConverseStream / InvokeModelWithResponseStream) reduce the delay before the first visible token, which is the perceived-latency signal users react to, even when total InvocationLatency is unchanged. Latency-optimized inference, cross-Region profiles, and Provisioned Throughput target actual processing time, resilience/throughput, and capacity respectively - not the gap between request sent and first token shown.

stem: A financial-advisory chatbot invokes a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock that is not custom or fine-tuned. Traffic is light and unpredictable, so there is no throttling and CloudWatch shows plenty of spare capacity. However, each individual response takes noticeably longer to generate than the team's latency target, even for short answers. A teammate proposes purchasing Provisioned Throughput to fix this. Why is Provisioned Throughput unlikely to solve the problem, and what should the team try instead?
options: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for steady, high-volume traffic; it does not shorten a single request's generation time - the team should try latency-optimized inference for the supported model instead
Provisioned Throughput is only available for batch inference jobs, so it cannot apply here at all
Provisioned Throughput already includes latency-optimized inference automatically, so the team should just increase the model unit count
Provisioned Throughput requires cross-Region inference profiles to function, so enabling one will also reduce per-request latency
explanation: Provisioned Throughput is a capacity/cost lever for steady, predictable, high-utilization workloads; it does not by itself reduce the time a single request takes to generate a response. When per-request latency itself is the problem for a supported model, latency-optimized inference serves the model on faster infrastructure to cut actual response time. The other options misstate how Provisioned Throughput works.

stem: A platform engineering team is writing internal guidance so other teams choose the right Bedrock performance lever. They need to name the ONE capability that reduces the actual end-to-end processing time of a single invocation - not just perceived responsiveness - by serving supported foundation models on infrastructure built for speed. Which capability is it?
options: Latency-optimized inference
Response streaming
Provisioned Throughput
Batch inference
explanation: Latency-optimized inference serves supported models on infrastructure built for speed, cutting actual response time. Streaming only changes when partial output becomes visible (perceived latency); Provisioned Throughput is a capacity/cost lever for steady demand; batch inference is an asynchronous bulk mode, not a single-invocation speed lever.

stem: A retail store associate's handheld assistant app on Amazon Bedrock already uses ConverseStream, so answers appear incrementally as they are generated. Associates still complain that full answers take too long to finish appearing on the small screen, and the underlying model supports Amazon Bedrock's dedicated low-latency serving option. What should the team add next to reduce the actual time the model spends generating the response?
options: Enable latency-optimized inference for the model
Enable response streaming again using a different SDK
Move the workload to batch inference for faster turnaround
Purchase Provisioned Throughput to guarantee available capacity
explanation: Streaming already addresses perceived latency; to cut the model's actual generation time, the team should enable latency-optimized inference for the supported model. Streaming cannot be meaningfully re-enabled with a different SDK, batch inference is for asynchronous bulk jobs, and Provisioned Throughput addresses capacity/cost, not per-request generation speed.

stem: One week before a product launch, a team finds that their narrow, high-volume classification feature - currently served by a mid-size foundation model on Amazon Bedrock - misses its latency target under peak load, even though CloudWatch shows no throttling and plenty of spare capacity; the model's own per-request generation time is the bottleneck. A colleague suggests distilling the current model into a smaller custom student model to speed things up. Data collection, training, and evaluation for that student model cannot realistically finish before launch. What is the more immediate lever to try first?
options: Swap in an existing smaller, faster off-the-shelf foundation model (e.g., Amazon Nova Micro) for the task, since it requires no training
Proceed with model distillation on an accelerated timeline
Purchase Provisioned Throughput sized for peak load
Move the classification calls to batch inference
explanation: Swapping to an already-available smaller model (for example, Amazon Nova Micro, which delivers the lowest-latency responses among the Nova models) is an immediate configuration change with no training cycle, unlike distillation, which requires collecting data and training a new student model. Because CloudWatch shows no throttling and spare capacity, Provisioned Throughput would not address the root cause (the model's inherent per-request generation time), and batch inference is asynchronous and unsuitable for a feature with a latency target.

stem: A team's Amazon Bedrock application invokes a foundation model that is supported by Bedrock's latency-optimized inference feature. The team wants to reduce the actual per-request response time without switching to a different model. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Enable response streaming for the requests
Request latency-optimized inference for the model
Enable prompt caching for the request
Move the workload to batch inference
explanation: Latency-optimized inference serves supported models on faster infrastructure to reduce actual per-request latency while keeping the same model, matching the stated constraint. Streaming only improves perceived latency, prompt caching mainly helps when a large static prefix is repeated across requests, and batch inference is asynchronous and unsuitable when a single request's response time matters.

stem: A team enables response streaming for their Amazon Bedrock chat application, and end users report the assistant feels more responsive. However, the CloudWatch InvocationLatency metric, which measures time from request submission to the final response byte, shows no measurable change before and after the switch. Which explanation is correct?
options: Streaming lowers perceived latency by delivering tokens as they are generated, but it does not change the actual total time required to generate the full response
The InvocationLatency metric only tracks Provisioned Throughput invocations, so on-demand streaming improvements are not reflected in it
Streaming reduces the number of tokens the model must generate, so InvocationLatency should have dropped and the team likely misconfigured the metric
Streaming can only reduce latency once cross-Region inference profiles are also enabled for the same model
explanation: Response streaming improves perceived latency (tokens appear sooner) without changing the actual time needed to generate the full response, so an end-to-end metric like InvocationLatency (defined by AWS as the time from when a request is sent to when the last token is received) stays flat, exactly what was observed. Bedrock separately publishes a TimeToFirstToken metric for streaming calls, which is the metric that actually improves with streaming - underscoring that InvocationLatency measures total generation time, not perceived responsiveness. The other options invent mechanisms, such as a metric scoped only to Provisioned Throughput, fewer tokens being generated, or a dependency on cross-Region profiles, that do not reflect how these features work.

stem: A high-volume content-moderation pre-filter on Amazon Bedrock only needs to output a single moderation label per item. The team wants to reduce both the per-request latency and the per-request cost of this narrow task, is willing to accept a small potential accuracy trade-off, and is not planning any custom training or fine-tuning. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Enable response streaming to shorten the perceived wait for each label
Evaluate and switch to a smaller, faster foundation model sized for this narrow task, using Bedrock model evaluation to confirm accuracy remains acceptable
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the current large model to guarantee lower latency
Enable prompt caching for the moderation prompt template
explanation: Switching to a smaller foundation model for a narrow task reduces both latency and cost, and Bedrock model evaluation is the documented way to confirm the smaller model's accuracy is still acceptable before the swap, without any custom training. Streaming only helps perceived latency, Provisioned Throughput on the same large model does not shrink its inherent per-token latency, and prompt caching mainly benefits large repeated static prefixes rather than this task's per-item cost and latency.

stem: An Amazon Bedrock application experiences ThrottlingException errors and degraded availability during unpredictable regional traffic spikes, even though average daily volume is well within account quotas. The team wants to increase the effective throughput and resilience of the on-demand model calls during these spikes without redesigning the application's request-handling logic. Which change is MOST appropriate?
options: Switch the application to invoke the model through a cross-Region inference profile
Reduce the max_tokens parameter on every request so each response completes faster
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model to guarantee steady, predictable capacity
Enable response streaming so users perceive faster responses during peak load
explanation: Cross-Region inference profiles raise effective throughput and resilience during spikes by routing on-demand traffic across Regions, directly addressing throttling during unpredictable bursts without any application redesign. Truncating output degrades functionality rather than fixing capacity, Provisioned Throughput suits steady predictable volume rather than bursty spikes, and streaming only changes perceived latency, not throttling.

stem: A live customer-support agent-assist panel calls an Amazon Bedrock model to draft suggested replies while an agent is on a call. Product wants the suggested text to begin appearing on the agent's screen as soon as possible after the request is sent, even though the full suggestion still takes several seconds to finish generating. Which change is MOST appropriate?
options: Switch the request from a standard (non-streaming) invocation to a streaming invocation, so tokens render incrementally as they are produced
Switch the model to a Provisioned Throughput deployment, which reserves dedicated capacity so the complete response returns faster
Enable prompt caching on the suggested-reply prompt template
Move the workload to batch inference for faster overall turnaround
explanation: Switching to a streaming invocation renders tokens incrementally as they are produced, so partial text appears on screen almost immediately even though the full response still takes time to complete. Provisioned Throughput and batch inference do not change how quickly partial output is rendered, and prompt caching mainly speeds up shared static prefixes rather than making tokens appear incrementally on screen.

stem: Which Amazon Bedrock latency lever is generally understood to reduce BOTH the actual response latency AND the per-request cost of a workload at the same time, at the potential expense of output quality on complex tasks?
options: Response streaming
Cross-Region inference profiles
Choosing a smaller foundation model sized for the task (for example, Amazon Nova Micro for lightweight classification)
Provisioned Throughput
explanation: A smaller foundation model reduces both actual latency and per-request cost simultaneously, at the risk of lower accuracy on complex tasks. Streaming only affects perceived latency, cross-Region inference profiles address throughput and resilience rather than cost, and Provisioned Throughput trades an hourly or term commitment for predictable capacity rather than an inherent cost reduction.

stem: A FinOps analyst building a starter cost dashboard for a new Amazon Bedrock on-demand application wants to alarm on the single CloudWatch metric that most directly reflects prompt size, since larger prompts drive up per-request token cost. Which metric should the alarm target?
options: InputTokenCount
OutputTokenCount
InvocationLatency
Invocations
explanation: InputTokenCount reports the number of tokens sent to the model in each request, the direct driver of prompt-side, on-demand cost. OutputTokenCount measures generated tokens (a separate cost driver), InvocationLatency measures response time rather than token volume, and Invocations counts calls but says nothing about request size.

stem: A team wants to be alerted specifically when their Amazon Bedrock DOLLAR spend is on pace to exceed a monthly target, not when API call volume crosses a count-based threshold. Which AWS Budgets budget type fits this need?
options: A cost budget tracking actual and forecasted Bedrock spend against a monthly dollar target
A usage budget tracking the number of Bedrock API calls against a monthly count target
An RI utilization budget tracking Reserved Instance usage
A CloudWatch composite alarm combining InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount
explanation: AWS Budgets cost budgets track actual and forecasted dollar spend against a target amount, matching the team's need. A usage budget tracks a quantity/count metric rather than dollars, an RI utilization budget applies to Reserved Instances (not relevant to on-demand Bedrock), and a CloudWatch alarm is a metric-threshold mechanism, not an AWS Budgets dollar-spend construct.

stem: A team's Amazon Bedrock bill keeps rising even though CloudWatch shows the Invocations and InputTokenCount metrics holding steady week over week. Which metric should they check next to explain the growth?
options: OutputTokenCount
InvocationLatency
InvocationClientErrors
InvocationThrottles
explanation: With call volume (Invocations) and prompt size (InputTokenCount) both flat, the remaining token-based cost driver is OutputTokenCount - the model may be generating longer completions per request. InvocationLatency measures response time, and InvocationClientErrors/InvocationThrottles reflect request failures and throttling, none of which explain steady, flat-volume spend growth.

stem: A team notices their monthly Amazon Bedrock bill has grown substantially. They check their CloudWatch dashboard and see that InvocationLatency has stayed flat and well within their performance target, so they conclude that billed usage itself must not have changed. Why is this conclusion unreliable, and what should they check instead?
options: InvocationLatency measures response time, not billed usage; they should check InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, and Invocations instead
InvocationLatency is unreliable in CloudWatch and should be ignored entirely
A flat InvocationLatency proves cost is flat, since Bedrock bills by response time under on-demand pricing
They should check Amazon S3 storage costs instead, since Bedrock bills are primarily driven by storage
explanation: On-demand Amazon Bedrock pricing is driven by tokens processed and number of requests, not by response time, so InvocationLatency is not a valid proxy for spend; the team should check InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, and Invocations instead. Latency remains a valid performance metric, just not a billing signal; Bedrock does not bill by response time; and Bedrock invocation cost is not primarily an S3 storage cost.

stem: A platform team wants two independent safeguards: (1) an alert within minutes if a single application's Bedrock token usage suddenly spikes, and (2) a separate alert if total Bedrock spend across the account is trending to exceed the monthly plan. Which pairing correctly matches each need to the right AWS capability?
options: CloudWatch alarms on Bedrock invocation metrics (such as InputTokenCount/OutputTokenCount) for need (1); AWS Budgets for need (2)
AWS Budgets for need (1); CloudWatch alarms on Bedrock invocation metrics for need (2)
AWS Trusted Advisor for both needs
AWS Cost and Usage Report parsed manually each morning for both needs
explanation: CloudWatch Bedrock metrics update near real time and are granular enough to catch a single application's usage spike, while AWS Budgets evaluates spend against a plan on a billing-cycle basis, making it the right fit for account-wide monthly trend alerts. Reversing the pairing mismatches each tool's strength, and neither Trusted Advisor nor a manually parsed Cost and Usage Report is a proactive alerting mechanism.
exclusionReason: Unresolved after source review: Single-app metric attribution requires a distinct app/profile/custom metric setup when multiple applications share one model.

stem: A small team running a pilot Amazon Bedrock application has no dedicated FinOps staff. They want an automated email alert if their monthly Amazon Bedrock spend is on pace to exceed a fixed dollar amount, without building any custom reporting. Which AWS capability should they configure?
options: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights queries run on a nightly schedule
AWS Budgets with a cost budget and an alert threshold
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging delivered to Amazon S3
explanation: AWS Budgets lets a team set a spend threshold and receive proactive alerts without building custom reporting. CloudWatch Logs Insights and invocation logging require the team to build and run their own analysis, and Trusted Advisor checks surface general cost-optimization recommendations rather than budget alerts.

stem: According to AWS guidance for Amazon Bedrock workloads, which combination of capabilities forms the recommended baseline for monitoring and controlling ongoing generative AI spend?
options: Amazon CloudWatch alarms on Bedrock usage metrics, paired with AWS Budgets for proactive spend alerts
AWS Config conformance packs, paired with AWS Security Hub findings
AWS X-Ray distributed tracing, paired with AWS CloudTrail event history
AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations, paired with AWS Trusted Advisor performance checks
explanation: CloudWatch alarms on Bedrock usage metrics (InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, Invocations) catch usage anomalies, while AWS Budgets delivers proactive spend alerts - together they form the standard cost-monitoring baseline. The other pairings target configuration compliance, distributed tracing/audit history, and compute/performance optimization, none of which are built for spend monitoring.

stem: A production application on Amazon Bedrock has an intermittent bug: a background job occasionally resubmits the same short, fixed-size prompt several times in a tight retry loop. The team wants a CloudWatch alarm that will unambiguously confirm a rise in retry count, independent of any change in prompt or response size. Which metric should the alarm target?
options: InputTokenCount, because it captures every token sent regardless of how many calls produced it
Invocations, because it counts API calls directly and is unaffected by how large each call's prompt or response is
InvocationLatency, because retries always increase the average response time
OutputTokenCount, because retries proportionally increase generated tokens too
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0664 for current practice. Invocations counts requests Bedrock accepts for processing, so Sum measures accepted request volume. It excludes throttled requests and requests rejected during input validation before processing. Token counts also depend on payload size, and latency measures time. Confirm actual retries using SDK telemetry or correlated request logs rather than request volume alone.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Changes the requirement to accepted call volume and explicitly separates it from retry-count confirmation.

stem: A summarization endpoint on Amazon Bedrock keeps its input prompts nearly constant in size, but a recent change to the system prompt causes the model to produce noticeably longer responses. Which CloudWatch metric captures this specific cost driver so the team can alarm on it going forward?
options: InputTokenCount
Invocations
OutputTokenCount
InvocationLatency
explanation: OutputTokenCount tracks generated-token volume, which is exactly what grows when responses get longer while prompt size and call volume stay flat. InputTokenCount and Invocations would stay flat in this scenario, and InvocationLatency reflects response time, not the token volume driving cost.

stem: A platform team wants two different things from their Amazon Bedrock cost tooling: first, to notice within minutes if a deployment bug causes a sudden burst of token usage so they can intervene quickly; second, to see partway through the month whether total Bedrock spend is on a trajectory that will land above the team's allocated monthly amount. Which pairing of AWS capabilities correctly matches each need?
options: Use AWS Budgets for the near-real-time burst detection and a CloudWatch alarm for the mid-month spend trend

Use a CloudWatch alarm on Bedrock usage metrics (such as InputTokenCount or Invocations) for the near-real-time burst detection, and AWS Budgets with a spend-threshold alert for the mid-month trend warning
Use Amazon Bedrock model evaluation for both needs
Use AWS Trusted Advisor for both needs
explanation: CloudWatch alarms on Bedrock usage metrics fire within minutes for anomaly detection, while AWS Budgets is built for spend-trend warnings over the course of a billing period - the two tools serve different time horizons and are not interchangeable. Swapping them misassigns near-real-time detection to a tool that evaluates spend periodically, and the other options are unrelated to cost monitoring.

stem: A retail company's product-review sentiment-tagging service on Amazon Bedrock invokes a large frontier model at very high daily volume. The frontier model already meets the accuracy bar; the only problem is per-request inference cost. Which technique is purpose-built for this exact pattern: a narrow task, high volume, and accuracy that is already sufficient?
options: Enable prompt caching on the sentiment-tagging prompt template.
Distill the frontier model's behavior on this task into a smaller, cheaper student model and serve that instead.
Turn on latency-optimized inference for the frontier model.
Add a cross-Region inference profile in front of the frontier model.
explanation: Model distillation is built exactly for a narrow, high-volume task where a frontier model already meets accuracy but costs too much: it transfers the teacher's behavior into a smaller, cheaper student model. Prompt caching only cuts cost when a large static prefix repeats across requests, which is not what drives cost here. Latency-optimized inference targets response speed, not per-token spend, and cross-Region inference profiles raise throughput and resilience, not cost.

stem: An engineering team fine-tunes Anthropic Claude 3 Haiku on Amazon Bedrock to create a custom model for a high-volume support-ticket tagging workload. Before production traffic can reach the fine-tuned model, what must the team provision?
options: Nothing - every custom model on Amazon Bedrock, including Claude-based ones, is automatically servable on-demand.
Provisioned Throughput for the fine-tuned model, since Claude custom (fine-tuned) models require Provisioned Throughput to serve inference traffic.
A cross-Region inference profile, since custom models cannot be invoked from a single fixed Region without one.
A Bedrock batch inference schedule, since custom models can only be invoked asynchronously.
