explanation: Claude custom (fine-tuned) models on Amazon Bedrock still require Provisioned Throughput to serve inference; only a narrow set of base models - such as PEFT-customized Amazon Nova models and Meta Llama 3.3 70B Instruct - can be deployed for on-demand inference after customization, and Claude is not among them. Custom models are not automatically on-demand, cross-Region inference profiles solve throughput and resilience rather than a deployment prerequisite, and batch inference is a separate asynchronous path, not a requirement for serving the model at all.

stem: A fintech team runs a narrow classification task on Amazon Bedrock at a modest, steady volume of a few thousand requests per day using a large frontier model. Inference cost is a minor line item, and the team has no in-house tooling to manage a custom model's lifecycle. A colleague proposes investing in model distillation to cut costs. What is the MOST important factor to weigh before committing to this proposal?
options: Whether the frontier model supports response streaming, since distillation requires streaming to be enabled first.

Whether the long-term savings from a smaller student model's lower per-token cost, and the operational overhead of maintaining a custom model, outweigh the one-time training effort at this request volume.
Whether the task can instead be moved to batch inference, since batch and distillation cannot both be used for the same workload.
Whether the frontier model's context window is large enough to fit the system prompt, since that determines whether distillation is technically possible.
explanation: Distillation is an investment: it pays off when the ongoing per-token savings and reduced serving cost outweigh the one-time training effort and the added operational burden of running a custom model, which matters more at modest volume than at very high volume. Streaming support, batch-versus-distillation exclusivity, and context window size are unrelated to whether distillation is worth pursuing.

stem: A support-operations team wants to shrink Bedrock inference cost for a high-volume FAQ-style question-answering task currently served by a frontier model. They do not have a large hand-labeled dataset of ideal answers, but they do have a large collection of representative user questions. Which capability of Amazon Bedrock model distillation makes this workable?
options: Distillation requires a pre-existing, human-labeled dataset of prompt-response pairs, so the team must label an ideal answer for every question before proceeding.
Distillation can invoke the frontier teacher model to generate the reference responses for the supplied prompts, so a hand-labeled ground-truth dataset is not strictly required.
Distillation only accepts training data captured from AWS CloudTrail management events.
Distillation cannot proceed unless the questions are first collapsed into a single static prompt using prompt caching.
explanation: Bedrock model distillation can use the teacher model itself to generate response data for a supplied set of prompts, so teams without a hand-labeled dataset can still distill using their existing representative questions. Distillation is not limited to human-labeled data, is unrelated to CloudTrail, and has no dependency on prompt caching.

stem: An e-commerce team's product-recommendation-reason generator on Amazon Bedrock writes a one-sentence reason for each recommended item, generated synchronously at request time as users browse the site. It handles one specific, well-defined task at extremely high volume using a frontier model that already produces reasons of acceptable quality. The team's only goal is to cut the per-request bill for this task while keeping quality about the same. What is the standard fix for exactly this pattern?
options: Raise the top-k value used during retrieval so each request includes more context.
Move all traffic for this task to Amazon Bedrock batch inference.
Distill the frontier model's behavior on this narrow task into a smaller student model and serve that instead.
Enable prompt caching on the recommendation prompt template.
explanation: A narrow, well-defined task running at very high volume where accuracy is already acceptable and only cost needs to drop is the textbook case for model distillation. Raising top-k is a RAG retrieval lever unrelated to this task, batch inference does not fit a synchronous, request-time response, and prompt caching only saves cost on a shared static prefix, not on the model's baseline per-token cost.

stem: A team uses a frontier foundation model on Amazon Bedrock to tag incoming product reviews into one of eight fixed categories as each review is submitted, and the classification result must be returned synchronously within the review-submission flow. The frontier model comfortably meets the required accuracy, but its per-request cost is too high at the team's daily review volume. Which approach is MOST appropriate to reduce cost while keeping the frontier model's accuracy on this specific task?
options: Distill the frontier model's behavior on this classification task into a smaller student model, and serve the student model instead.
Enable prompt caching on the frontier model's system instructions.
Submit the review-tagging requests as an asynchronous batch inference job.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the frontier model at its current size.
explanation: Model distillation is designed exactly for this pattern - a narrow, high-volume task where a frontier model already meets accuracy but costs too much - by transferring its task-specific behavior into a cheaper student model. Prompt caching only discounts repeated static tokens rather than right-sizing the model, batch inference is asynchronous and unsuitable for a synchronous review-submission flow, and Provisioned Throughput on the unchanged frontier model keeps its full cost profile instead of reducing it.
exclusionReason: Unresolved after source review: Distillation is a means to approach task accuracy, not a guarantee of identical or lossless teacher accuracy.

stem: A team runs a narrow, high-volume support-ticket urgency classifier on a frontier model on Amazon Bedrock that meets their accuracy bar, but at high cost. As a cheaper alternative, they pilot a much smaller pre-built foundation model with no adaptation, and its raw accuracy on this task falls well below what is required. Which approach lets them move to a smaller, cheaper model while keeping accuracy close to the frontier model's on this specific task?
options: Deploy the small pre-built model as-is and accept the lower accuracy.
Distill the frontier model's task-specific behavior into a smaller student model, then serve the tuned student model.
Add more few-shot examples to the prompt sent to the small pre-built model.
Enable cross-Region inference profiles for the small pre-built model.
explanation: Distillation transfers the teacher (frontier) model's task-specific behavior into a smaller student model so it approaches teacher-level accuracy on that narrow task, which a plain model swap does not achieve. More few-shot examples raise prompt cost and latency without transferring the teacher's learned behavior, and cross-Region inference profiles address throughput and resilience, not per-task accuracy.

stem: A team distills a frontier teacher model on Amazon Bedrock into a smaller student model whose model family has not been granted an on-demand exception for custom models. Traffic to the resulting classification workload is steady and predictable in production. How should the team serve the distilled student model?
options: Invoke the distilled student model on-demand, the same way they would invoke a base foundation model.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the distilled student model.
Route all production requests to the distilled student model through a nightly batch inference job.
Continue serving the original frontier teacher model and discard the distilled student model.
explanation: Like most custom (fine-tuned or distilled) models on Bedrock, the student model generally requires Provisioned Throughput to serve, unless its specific model family has been granted an on-demand exception for custom models. On-demand invocation, routing everything through an offline batch job, or abandoning the distilled model all contradict the point of distillation or the serving rule for custom models.

stem: An extraction pipeline on Amazon Bedrock uses a frontier model to pull five structured fields from long, narrow-domain contracts. The team already places a prompt-cache checkpoint after the shared instructions, which lowered time-to-first-token and input-token billing, but the per-invocation cost of the large frontier model itself remains the dominant cost driver. Invocation traffic is bursty and unpredictable, so Provisioned Throughput's steady-utilization requirement is not met. Which action MOST directly reduces the remaining cost while preserving the frontier model's field-extraction accuracy on this narrow task?
options: Add a second cache checkpoint further into the prompt.
Increase the maximum output token limit for the extraction responses.
Distill the frontier model's field-extraction behavior into a smaller student model and serve that instead.
Move the workload from on-demand to Provisioned Throughput for the same frontier model.
explanation: Because contracts differ per request, additional cache checkpoints yield little further savings, and the large model's own inference cost - not the shared prefix - is now the bottleneck; distillation replaces the frontier model with a cheaper student model that keeps this narrow task's accuracy. Raising the output token limit does not reduce cost, and Provisioned Throughput is explicitly ruled out by the bursty, unpredictable traffic pattern.
exclusionReason: Unresolved after source review: Distillation is a means to approach task accuracy, not a guarantee of identical or lossless teacher accuracy.

stem: A team is deciding whether model distillation is a good fit for two different Amazon Bedrock workloads: (1) a narrow, high-volume ticket-priority classifier that already meets accuracy on a frontier model but costs too much to run at scale, and (2) an open-ended, general-purpose research assistant that handles unpredictable, multi-topic conversations at low volume. For which workload is model distillation the MOST appropriate optimization?
options: Workload 2 only, the general-purpose research assistant.
Workload 1 only, the narrow, high-volume classifier.
Both workloads equally.
Neither workload; use prompt caching for both instead.
explanation: Distillation is built for narrow, high-volume tasks where a frontier model's accuracy is well characterized and can be transferred into a cheaper student model. A broad, unpredictable, low-volume conversational workload does not fit this pattern and does not justify the training investment distillation requires.

stem: A content-moderation pipeline on Amazon Bedrock uses a frontier model to flag policy-violating text across a fixed set of violation categories. The frontier model already exceeds the required accuracy, but the team's monthly Bedrock bill for this single narrow task is the largest line item in their AI budget due to high daily message volume. Which Bedrock capability is designed specifically to move this task to a smaller model without losing the frontier model's task-specific accuracy?
options: Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock
Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock
Model distillation
Amazon Bedrock Agents
explanation: Model distillation is purpose-built to transfer a frontier teacher model's task-specific accuracy into a cheaper, smaller student model for narrow, high-volume tasks like this one. Guardrails filter content for safety, Knowledge Bases add retrieval-augmented context, and Agents orchestrate multi-step tool use - none of them right-size the model to reduce cost.
exclusionReason: Unresolved after source review: Distillation is a means to approach task accuracy, not a guarantee of identical or lossless teacher accuracy.

stem: A team currently pays contract reviewers to manually check every one of 5,000 weekly spam or not-spam labels a Bedrock-based classifier produces, comparing each label against an established list of confirmed-correct answers. Cost is climbing, and each check is a simple label comparison, not a subjective judgment call. What should the team do?
options: Replace the human evaluation job with an automatic evaluation job using exact-match or F1 against the confirmed-correct labels
Replace the human evaluation job with an LLM-as-a-judge job scoring the classifier's reasoning
Keep the human evaluation job, since it is the most accurate option and label correctness is a compliance requirement
Add a canary rollout comparing the classifier's live labels against a shadow deployment
explanation: Because each check is a simple, objective comparison against an already-confirmed label rather than a subjective judgment call, an automatic evaluation job using exact-match or F1 gives the same signal for a fraction of the cost and effort. Keeping costly human review for a purely objective comparison misapplies a method meant for subjective, high-stakes judgment, an LLM-as-a-judge job adds unnecessary machinery for scoring reasoning nobody needs judged, and a canary rollout addresses live traffic routing, not label-checking cost.

stem: A team ran an automatic (reference-based) Amazon Bedrock evaluation job on a new creative-writing assistant and the aggregate BERTScore came back high. Manual spot checks, however, show many responses are repetitive and off-brand in tone. What should the team do to get a quality signal that actually reflects this problem?
options: Increase the number of gold reference outputs used by the automatic evaluation job
Replace or supplement the automatic evaluation job with an LLM-as-a-judge job scoring dimensions like tone and originality against the team's own prompt dataset
Lower the model's inference temperature and rerun the same automatic evaluation job
Re-run the identical automatic evaluation job on a larger sample of the same prompts
explanation: BERTScore uses contextual BERT embeddings and cosine similarity to measure semantic similarity against reference text; it is not just lexical overlap. That score alone does not establish factual faithfulness, coherence, empathy or brand tone. Choose a rubric-based judge or human review where those dimensions matter, and calibrate the evaluation on representative cases.

stem: Which TWO of the following statements correctly describe an Amazon Bedrock LLM-as-a-judge evaluation job? (Select TWO.)
options: It requires a set of gold reference outputs to compute its scores
It can score nuanced dimensions such as coherence, faithfulness, and conciseness using the team's own prompt dataset
It is the go-to choice for scoring automatically on every release across thousands of items
It is reserved for infrequent, high-stakes sign-off because it is too slow and costly to repeat often
It measures only lexical or surface-level overlap between a response and a reference answer
explanation: LLM-as-a-judge brings your own prompt dataset and scores nuanced dimensions at scale, making it the go-to method for automatic evaluation on every release. It does not require gold reference outputs, that describes automatic reference-based metrics, it is not the slow, infrequent option, that describes human evaluation, and it is not limited to surface-level overlap, which also describes reference-based metrics.

stem: A pharmaceutical company must certify, for a regulatory submission, that a Bedrock-generated patient-facing drug-interaction summary meets accuracy and tone requirements. Licensed pharmacists review a small quarterly sample rather than every generated summary. Which TWO statements correctly describe the evaluation job type used here? (Select TWO.)
options: It routes responses to the company's own subject-matter experts for rating against defined criteria
It is generally the most accurate evaluation approach, but too slow and costly to repeat on every release
It scores thousands of items automatically on every release using the team's own prompt dataset
It requires gold reference outputs to compute an overlap-based score
It is the deterministic, repeatable regression gate meant to run on every pull request
explanation: This is a human evaluation job: it routes the sample to the company's own subject-matter experts, the licensed pharmacists, and is the most accurate option but reserved for infrequent, high-stakes review rather than every release. Scoring thousands of items automatically every release describes LLM-as-a-judge, requiring gold reference outputs describes automatic reference-based metrics, and a deterministic per-pull-request gate describes the golden-dataset CI pattern, not human evaluation.

stem: A summarization team scored a new model release with BERTScore against a set of reference summaries and saw high overlap scores. After release, users reported that many summaries were incoherent and missed the article's main point. What explains the mismatch, and what should the team change about its evaluation approach?
options: BERTScore is deprecated; the team should switch to computing an F1 score against the same references instead
Reference-based metrics measure surface-level overlap with the reference text and do not capture coherence or faithfulness; the team should add LLM-as-a-judge scoring to evaluate those dimensions
The reference summaries were generated by the wrong foundation model, so the team should regenerate them using the model under test
The team should switch entirely to human evaluation for every future weekly release, since it is strictly more accurate
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0665 for current practice. BERTScore uses contextual BERT embeddings and cosine similarity to measure semantic similarity against reference text; it is not just lexical overlap. That score alone does not establish factual faithfulness, coherence, empathy or brand tone. Choose a rubric-based judge or human review where those dimensions matter, and calibrate the evaluation on representative cases.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Resolve the source-audited accuracy issue without changing a published answer key.

stem: A team is evaluating an open-ended customer-question answering assistant. Because many different phrasings can be equally correct, the team has no single canonical answer to use as a gold reference for most questions, yet they still need to score thousands of responses automatically after every deployment. Which evaluation job type should they choose, and why?
options: Automatic (reference-based) metrics, because BERTScore can be computed without any reference text
LLM-as-a-judge, because it scores response quality against a prompt dataset rather than requiring gold reference outputs
Human evaluation, because only human reviewers can judge open-ended answers
Automatic (reference-based) metrics, because the F1 score is unaffected by paraphrasing away from the reference text
explanation: The scenario has no usable gold references, so a calibrated LLM judge with the specified rubric is the best listed automatic approach. BERTScore and F1 require reference data for these reference-based comparisons. BERTScore is embedding-based and can accommodate semantic paraphrases; the absence of reference answers, rather than lexical wording differences alone, is the relevant limitation.

stem: A startup just launched a grief-support chatbot. To save time, the team plans to reuse a set of human-graded reference summaries from an unrelated dataset and run automatic reference-based metrics on every nightly build to catch regressions in the chatbot's tone and empathy. What is the flaw in this plan?
options: There is no flaw; automatic reference-based metrics reliably score tone and empathy because they compare against human-graded references

Automatic reference-based metrics measure textual overlap with the reference and poorly capture nuanced qualities like tone and empathy; the team should use LLM-as-a-judge for routine checks, and reserve human evaluation for high-stakes sign-off given the sensitivity of this use case
The team should switch to Provisioned Throughput to guarantee consistent latency, which will resolve the tone concern
The team should set temperature to 0 so every nightly response matches the reference text exactly
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0666 for current practice. Reference metrics must match the task and dataset: BERTScore captures contextual semantic similarity, not a complete measure of empathy or safe support behavior. An unrelated summarization dataset is also a poor benchmark. Use a representative support dataset, a calibrated rubric-based judge for routine signals, and appropriate ongoing human safety oversight. Temperature zero can reduce variability on supported models; it does not force a response to match a reference.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Resolve the source-audited accuracy issue without changing a published answer key.

stem: A generative AI platform team is designing its overall evaluation strategy across the release lifecycle. Which two statements accurately describe when to use each Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job type? (Choose 2)
options: LLM-as-a-judge is well suited to automatically scoring thousands of responses on dimensions such as coherence and faithfulness every release
Human evaluation should replace automated evaluation for every weekly release because it is unconditionally the most accurate method
Automatic (reference-based) metrics are ideal for scoring open-ended, creative responses where many different answers are equally correct
Human evaluation should be reserved for subjective, high-stakes sign-off, such as brand voice or legal tone review, where mistakes carry outsized risk
Automatic (reference-based) metrics require no gold reference outputs and directly measure whether an answer is grounded in retrieved context
explanation: LLM-as-a-judge scales to automated, nuanced scoring on every release, and human evaluation is reserved for subjective, high-stakes sign-off where a judge model is not authoritative enough. Human evaluation is too slow and costly to run on every release, automatic reference-based metrics need a fixed reference so they suit open-ended creative tasks poorly, and those metrics require gold references rather than needing none.

stem: A team evaluates a RAG assistant used for internal product-documentation search. For a batch of test questions, the Knowledge Bases RAG evaluation job reports high context relevance and high faithfulness, but low helpfulness. Manual review confirms the retrieved passages are correct and every sentence in the generated answers is fully supported by them, yet the answers ramble through general background material instead of directly answering the specific question asked. What should the team change first?
options: Re-chunk and re-ingest the knowledge base with a smaller chunk size to improve retrieval precision.
Replace the embeddings model used to build the vector index.
Revise the generation prompt to instruct the model to answer the specific question directly and concisely, using the retrieved context only as supporting material.
Attach a denied-topics guardrail policy to block off-topic content.
explanation: High context relevance and high faithfulness show retrieval and factual support are both fine, so the fault is that the model is not directly addressing the question, an instruction-following issue best fixed by tightening the generation prompt. Retrieval changes such as re-chunking or a new embeddings model would not fix a model that ignores instructions, and a denied-topics guardrail blocks disallowed subject matter, not verbose-but-on-topic answers.

stem: A team configures a Bedrock guardrail's contextual grounding check with a grounding threshold of 0.9 and a relevance threshold of 0.5. A production response scores 0.95 for groundedness, well above the grounding threshold, but only 0.4 for relevance, below the relevance threshold. What happens to this response?
options: It is allowed through, because the grounding score, which is weighted more heavily, is well above its threshold.
It is allowed through, because only the average of the two scores needs to clear a single combined threshold.
It is blocked only if both scores fall below their thresholds simultaneously.
It is blocked, because the guardrail blocks a response if either the grounding score or the relevance score falls below its configured threshold, even if the other score is well above its threshold.
explanation: The contextual grounding check evaluates grounding and relevance independently against their own configured thresholds, and a response is filtered if either score falls short, so a high grounding score does not compensate for a low relevance score. There is no weighting scheme, no single averaged threshold, and blocking is not conditioned on both scores failing at once.

stem: A team is documenting how to interpret Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG evaluation output for new engineers. Which TWO statements are correct?
options: Context relevance measures whether the retrieved passages are on topic for the question, so a low score points to a retrieval problem.

Faithfulness measures whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved passages, so high context relevance paired with low faithfulness indicates the model is adding unsupported content during generation.
A low faithfulness score is best fixed by ingesting additional source documents into the knowledge base.
Completeness measures whether the retrieved passages are on topic for the question.
High context relevance guarantees that the final generated answer is factually accurate.
explanation: Context relevance isolates retrieval quality, and pairing high context relevance with low faithfulness pinpoints a generation-side hallucination fault rather than a retrieval fault. Low faithfulness is a generation problem best addressed with a grounding-focused prompt, lower temperature, or a guardrail rather than more documents; the on-topic check belongs to context relevance, not completeness, and strong retrieval alone does not guarantee a faithful, accurate answer.

stem: A RAG evaluation job for an HR-policy assistant reports low context relevance but high faithfulness for a batch of test questions. Manual review confirms every generated answer is fully supported by whatever passages were retrieved, yet the answers still fail to correctly resolve the users' questions. What does this combination MOST likely indicate, and what should the team do?
options: The model is hallucinating, so the fix is a grounding-focused prompt or lower temperature.
Because faithfulness is high, no action is needed and the assistant is performing correctly.

The retriever is returning passages that are off topic for the question, and the model is faithfully summarizing that irrelevant content; the fix is a retrieval-side change such as re-chunking, tuning metadata filters, or evaluating the embeddings model.
The evaluation job double-counted the faithfulness score as the context relevance score, so the job should simply be re-run.
explanation: Low context relevance with high faithfulness means the model is faithful to whatever it retrieved, but the retrieved passages are the wrong ones for the question, so the fault sits in retrieval rather than generation. A hallucination-focused fix does not apply here because faithfulness is already high, and dismissing the result as fine or as a scoring glitch ignores a genuine, measurable retrieval gap.

stem: A user asks a RAG assistant about the return policy for a specific product line. The Bedrock Knowledge Bases evaluation job for this query shows high context relevance and high groundedness, but low correctness, because the retrieved passages actually describe the return policy for a different, similarly named product line and the model faithfully summarized them. Which statement correctly explains why groundedness stayed high despite the wrong answer?
options: Groundedness only checks that the answer is supported by whatever passages were retrieved, regardless of whether those passages actually answer the question
Groundedness and context relevance are computed from the same underlying score, so they always move together
Groundedness failed to detect the error because the guardrail's grounding threshold was set too low
Groundedness is invalid whenever context relevance is measured on the wrong product line
explanation: Groundedness (Bedrock's Faithfulness metric) only verifies that the generated text is faithful to the retrieved passages; it says nothing about whether those passages actually address the user's question or whether the answer is right, which is what the correctness metric captures. The other options invent a coupling between metrics or a guardrail failure that is not how the metric works.

stem: A knowledge base ingests a legacy internal wiki that contains an outdated pricing table. A RAG assistant answers a pricing question by faithfully quoting that outdated table, and the Bedrock Knowledge Bases evaluation job scores the response with high groundedness. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The high groundedness score guarantees the answer is factually correct in the real world

Groundedness only confirms the answer is supported by the retrieved content, not that the retrieved content itself is accurate or current, so stale source documents can still produce a high-groundedness but wrong answer
The evaluation job must be misconfigured, because groundedness cannot be high when an answer is factually wrong
This indicates a low context relevance problem that requires re-embedding the knowledge base
explanation: Groundedness measures faithfulness to the retrieved passages, not truth against the real world; if the source documents are stale, a faithful answer can still be wrong. The fix here is data freshness in the knowledge base, not a metric malfunction or a context relevance issue.

stem: A team enables an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with the contextual grounding check on its RAG assistant, expecting unsupported answers to be blocked. Weeks later, users still occasionally receive confident answers that invent statistics not present in any retrieved passage. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: Contextual grounding check only applies to Knowledge Bases evaluation jobs, not to live guardrail enforcement
The guardrail's grounding and relevance thresholds are set too permissively, allowing weakly supported responses through
Groundedness cannot be enforced by a guardrail and requires a custom Lambda function instead
The knowledge base's context relevance score is too high for the guardrail to act on
explanation: Contextual grounding check compares a response's grounding and relevance scores against configured thresholds; if those thresholds are set too low, weakly grounded responses still pass. It does operate on live invocations, not just offline evaluation, and it does not require a custom Lambda function.

stem: A Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG evaluation job reports low groundedness with high context relevance across a batch of test queries. Which two actions directly target the identified fault? (Select TWO.)
options: Add a grounding-focused instruction to the system prompt so the model is told to answer only from the retrieved context
Attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with the contextual grounding check enabled and set an appropriate grounding threshold
Increase the number of retrieved passages (top-k) sent to the model
Re-embed the knowledge base with a different embeddings model
Increase the maximum token limit for the generated response
explanation: Low groundedness with high context relevance is a generation fault, so the effective fixes are generation-side: a grounding-focused prompt and a guardrail that enforces contextual grounding checks. Changing top-k, embeddings, or the response token limit are retrieval or formatting changes that do not address unsupported content.

stem: A streaming media company operates a production Bedrock-based recommendation-blurb generator whose system prompt changes frequently. Which two practices together provide genuine prompt regression protection for this workload? (Choose 2)
options: Run an automated evaluation against a versioned golden dataset on every pull request and fail the build if the aggregate quality score drops below a defined threshold
After a prompt change passes offline evaluation, route a small percentage of live traffic to it and compare quality and business metrics against the current version before ramping up
Store every prompt revision in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management so a previous version can be restored if needed
Deploy every prompt change to 100 percent of production traffic immediately and monitor the invocation error rate for anomalies
Require a one-time human evaluation sign-off before the very first production launch, with no further checks on later changes
explanation: The documented discipline is a golden-dataset CI gate to catch regressions before merge plus a canary or A-B rollout to limit exposure afterward. Storing versions in Prompt Management enables rollback but does not evaluate or block anything, immediate 100 percent deployment with only error-rate monitoring skips staged exposure and measures the wrong signal, and a one-time launch sign-off provides no protection against later prompt edits.

stem: A gaming company's chat companion feature updates its system prompt several times per week. Quality is currently checked only through a quarterly manual audit, during which the team discovers that several intermediate prompt versions had degraded tone consistency months earlier without anyone noticing. Which change would let the team catch a quality regression as soon as it is introduced?
options: Add an automated evaluation against a versioned golden dataset that runs on every pull request and fails the build when the aggregate score drops below a defined threshold
Increase the frequency of the manual QA audit from quarterly to monthly
Replace the quarterly audit with a single human evaluation performed only before the initial feature launch
Rely on Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management's version history to automatically flag which revision caused the regression
explanation: Only an automated, CI-gated evaluation on every pull request catches a regression at the moment it is introduced, regardless of audit cadence. A monthly audit is still periodic and can miss regressions between cycles, a pre-launch-only check does nothing for later edits, and Prompt Management stores versions but performs no quality evaluation or flagging.

stem: A scheduling assistant's team has a new prompt version that already cleared the CI quality gate. To validate it under real user conditions with minimal risk, an engineer proposes immediately splitting production traffic 50/50 between the old and new prompt versions for exactly one hour, then cutting over completely regardless of the comparison outcome. What is the flaw in this plan?
options: The rollout should start with a small percentage of live traffic rather than a 50/50 split, and the team should compare quality and business metrics before ramping up instead of cutting over unconditionally after a fixed time
Canary rollouts are unnecessary once a change has passed the CI quality gate, so any live traffic split is wasted effort
A 50/50 split is required by Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management before a new prompt version can be marked as the default variant
The comparison window must run for at least 30 days because Bedrock evaluation jobs cannot process live traffic any faster
explanation: A canary or A-B rollout is meant to limit the blast radius, which means starting with a small percentage of traffic and ramping up only after quality and business metrics look acceptable, not committing to an unconditional cutover on a fixed timer. Passing the offline CI gate does not make a live comparison unnecessary, and neither the 50/50 split nor a 30-day minimum is an actual constraint of the discipline.

stem: A media company's editorial-assistant prompt changes are proposed through pull requests roughly twice a week. The team wants to both catch quality regressions automatically before any change merges and limit the impact of any regression that slips past that check. Which two-stage process satisfies both goals, in the correct order?
options: First route 10 percent of production traffic to every proposed prompt change, then run the golden-dataset evaluation only if the canary succeeds.

Run an automated golden-dataset evaluation on every pull request that fails the build when quality drops below a threshold, then after merge route a small percentage of live traffic to the new prompt and compare quality and business metrics before ramping up.
Run a one-time human evaluation on every pull request, then deploy directly to 100 percent of traffic.
Store each prompt version in Bedrock Prompt management and rely on its built-in quality scoring to decide whether to merge.
explanation: The deterministic pre-merge gate (golden dataset plus an automated per-pull-request evaluation) should run first to catch regressions before code ships, followed by a canary or A-B rollout that limits blast radius for anything the offline check misses. Canarying unvetted changes before the offline gate exposes real users first, a one-time human review does not scale as a repeatable CI gate, and Prompt management has no built-in quality scoring.

stem: A platform team is designing a regression-prevention process for a Bedrock-based writing assistant whose system prompt changes frequently. Which TWO practices should be part of this process? (Select TWO.)
options: Maintain a versioned golden dataset of representative inputs and run an automated evaluation on every pull request, failing the build if the aggregate quality score drops below a defined threshold.
After a prompt change passes offline evaluation, route a small percentage of live traffic to it and compare quality and business metrics against the current version before ramping up.
Store each prompt revision in Bedrock Prompt management and treat successful storage as proof the change is safe to ship.
Monitor only the Amazon Bedrock invocation error rate after deployment and treat a flat error rate as confirmation that quality is unchanged.
Skip pre-merge evaluation for minor wording tweaks, since only large prompt rewrites can cause a quality regression.
explanation: A versioned golden dataset with an automated per-pull-request evaluation gate, plus a canary or A-B rollout that compares quality and business metrics after the offline check passes, together form a deterministic pre-merge gate and a blast-radius limiter in production. Storing prompts in Prompt management alone proves nothing about quality, a flat error rate does not confirm quality is unchanged, and even small wording tweaks can cause regressions.

stem: An engineer sees a spike of ThrottlingException on a production Bedrock endpoint and, assuming the account lost access to the model, revokes and re-grants model access in the Bedrock console. After the change, the same error continues at the same rate with no improvement. What is actually happening, and what is the correct fix?
options: This is a rate-limiting problem, not an access problem; implement exponential backoff with jitter and consider requesting a quota increase or Provisioned Throughput
This is a permission problem; the IAM policy needs bedrock:InvokeModel added
This is an input-validation problem; the prompt needs to be chunked
This is a latency problem; compare InvocationLatency to internal timers to localize the bottleneck
explanation: The engineer applied the AccessDeniedException remedy (model access) to a ThrottlingException, which is a rate-limit problem with its own fix: backoff with jitter, and a quota increase or Provisioned Throughput for sustained load. Re-granting access, editing IAM, or chunking the prompt are remedies for different exceptions and do nothing for throttling.

stem: A team's Bedrock-backed pipeline is hitting ThrottlingException with increasing frequency as traffic grows, and demand is expected to keep rising through a major launch in two weeks. Beyond adding backoff with jitter to individual retries, which TWO actions are appropriate durable remedies for this sustained load? (Select 2.)
options: Grant model access again in the Bedrock console
Request a Bedrock service quota increase for the model's rate limit
Switch all requests to use CloudTrail logging instead of model invocation logging
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model to guarantee dedicated capacity
Reduce the IAM role's permissions to only bedrock:InvokeModel
explanation: For sustained demand that keeps producing ThrottlingException, the two durable remedies are requesting a service quota increase or purchasing Provisioned Throughput. Re-granting model access addresses AccessDeniedException, and the logging or IAM-trimming options have no effect on rate limits.

stem: During a load test, a Bedrock-backed API returns ThrottlingException on roughly 5 percent of calls at peak concurrency. Retrying the failed calls immediately in a tight loop makes the overall error rate worse, not better. Which retry strategy correctly addresses this pattern?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop to minimize latency impact on the user
Use exponential backoff with jitter so retries spread out over time instead of synchronizing into new bursts
Stop retrying and instead reduce the prompt size via chunking
Stop retrying and instead re-request model access for the account
explanation: Immediate tight-loop retries synchronize into new request bursts that worsen throttling; exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries out and is the documented client-side fix for ThrottlingException. Chunking and model access address ValidationException and AccessDeniedException, which are not the failure observed here.

stem: A developer is writing internal documentation to help on-call engineers stop confusing ThrottlingException with AccessDeniedException. Which TWO statements belong in that documentation as accurate? (Select 2.)
options: Both exceptions should always be fixed by requesting a service quota increase

ThrottlingException is typically intermittent and worsens at peak load, while a new model failing every single call immediately after being added usually indicates AccessDeniedException from missing model access
ThrottlingException means the prompt exceeded the model's context window
AccessDeniedException caused by missing model access is fixed in the Bedrock console, a setting separate from the IAM policy
AccessDeniedException is always transient and resolves itself after a short backoff delay
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0667 for current practice. Throttling concerns request/token quotas and calls for bounded backoff plus demand/capacity management. AccessDenied requires inspection of the actual policy and model activation state; many models activate automatically, with Marketplace or provider prerequisites where applicable. Not every AccessDenied is fixed by a console toggle, and pending activation can temporarily delay successful calls.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Resolve the source-audited accuracy issue without changing a published answer key.

stem: A team wraps all Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel calls in a generic retry decorator that applies exponential backoff with jitter to any exception, including ValidationException. Over the following weeks, a subset of requests with prompts approaching the model's maximum context length consistently exhausts all retry attempts and fails, consuming retry budget and adding latency before finally erroring out. What is the BEST way to fix this behavior?
options: Stop retrying ValidationException and instead reduce the offending input size through chunking or hierarchical summarization.
Increase the maximum number of retry attempts so the request eventually succeeds.
Add a longer maximum backoff ceiling so the jitter window is wider.
Move the retry decorator to run at the orchestration layer instead of the client layer.
explanation: ValidationException reflects a fixed input constraint (like an oversized prompt) that will fail identically on every attempt, so applying the ThrottlingException remedy of backoff and jitter only wastes retry budget and adds latency. The correct fix is to stop retrying and shrink the input via chunking or hierarchical summarization; more attempts, wider jitter, or relocating the decorator do not change the outcome.

stem: A team is designing a unified error-handling strategy for a production application that calls Amazon Bedrock and periodically encounters ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException, and ValidationException. Which two statements correctly describe how to handle these exceptions? (Select TWO.)
options: ThrottlingException should be retried with exponential backoff and jitter, and if the demand is sustained, addressed with a service quota increase or Provisioned Throughput.
A ValidationException caused by an oversized prompt should be resolved by reducing input size through chunking or hierarchical summarization, not by retrying.
AccessDeniedException should always be resolved by updating the calling IAM role's policy, since Bedrock authorizes every request through IAM alone.
ValidationException is transient like ThrottlingException, so it should be retried with the same exponential backoff and jitter strategy.
An AccessDeniedException that appears on every call to one newly added model, while an existing IAM role already succeeds against other models, should first be diagnosed as an IAM policy defect.
explanation: ThrottlingException is a rate-limit issue fixed with backoff and jitter, escalating to a quota increase or Provisioned Throughput for sustained load, and ValidationException is a fixed input-constraint error that must be fixed by shrinking the input, not retried. The other options are traps: AccessDeniedException is often caused by missing Bedrock model access rather than IAM alone, and treating ValidationException as transient wastes retries on a request that will always fail identically.

stem: A nightly batch job spins up 200 worker processes that each call the same Bedrock model at the top of the hour. Many workers receive ThrottlingException and all retry after exactly the same fixed exponential delay, causing a second wave of simultaneous requests that is throttled again, and the job frequently fails to complete even though the account's average call volume is well within its quota. What change would MOST directly fix this pattern?
options: Add random jitter to the exponential backoff delay so retries from different workers are spread out over time.
Increase the fixed exponential backoff multiplier so each retry waits longer than the last.
Reduce the number of retry attempts each worker is allowed to make.
Request a service quota increase, since the account is being throttled despite adequate average volume.
explanation: The symptom is a retry storm: synchronized fixed-delay retries recreate the same spike that caused the original throttling. Adding jitter desynchronizes retries across workers, spreading requests out so they succeed; a larger fixed multiplier, fewer attempts, or a quota increase do not address the synchronization problem causing repeated bursts.

stem: A team attaches a brand-new IAM role to a Lambda function that calls three different Bedrock foundation models, all of which the team has already enabled model access for in the console. Every call to all three models fails immediately with AccessDeniedException. What is the MOST likely root cause?
options: The IAM role is missing the bedrock:InvokeModel permission needed to call any model.
One of the three models has an unusually large context window that triggers ValidationException.
The account is being throttled because three models are being called concurrently.
Model access was granted in the wrong Region for all three models simultaneously.
explanation: When AccessDeniedException affects every model for a brand-new role, and model access is already confirmed enabled for all of them, the pattern points to a missing IAM permission such as bedrock:InvokeModel rather than a single model's access grant, since a model-access gap would typically affect one model while others still work. ValidationException and ThrottlingException produce different symptoms, and a Region mismatch would not plausibly occur identically across three independent enablements.

stem: After a RAG assistant returns a wrong answer, a developer confirms the correct passage is present in the knowledge base's source document. Before rewriting the generation prompt or adding few-shot examples to fix the wrong answer, what should the developer check?
options: Whether the passage is actually returned by the Retrieve API for that query, since a retrieval miss cannot be fixed by tuning generation
Whether the foundation model's context window is large enough to hold the entire source document
Whether a guardrail's denied topics configuration is filtering the model's response
Whether the model's temperature parameter is set above zero
explanation: When the correct passage exists but is never surfaced by Retrieve, the fault is in retrieval, not generation, so prompt or few-shot changes will not fix it; confirming what Retrieve actually returns isolates the failing stage first. Context window size, guardrail topic filters, and temperature are generation-side concerns and are irrelevant if the passage was never retrieved.

stem: A support team confirms that the passage needed to answer a customer question exists in the knowledge base's source document, but the Retrieve API never returns it for that question. Which TWO of the following are the usual root causes to investigate? (Choose 2.)
options: A metadata filter expression that does not match the document's actual attributes, silently excluding it from the candidate set
A chunking strategy that splits the answer's key facts from the query's key terms, leaving no chunk whose embedding is close enough to be retrieved
The generation model hallucinating an answer instead of using the retrieved context
The model's temperature parameter being set too high
A guardrail blocking the final response before it reaches the user
explanation: The two usual culprits for a passage that exists but is never returned by Retrieve are a metadata filter that does not match the document's attributes and a chunking strategy that separates key facts from query terms. Hallucination, temperature, and guardrail blocking are generation- or output-stage issues that occur after retrieval, not causes of a retrieval miss.

stem: A Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG assistant scopes every Retrieve call with a metadata filter equivalent to department = 'HR' so that each business unit only sees its own documents. After a policy document is migrated from a legacy content system into the S3 data source and re-synced, HR users report that the assistant can no longer surface that policy, even though a direct search of the S3 bucket confirms the file is present and correctly chunked. What should the team check first?
options: Whether the migrated document's metadata attributes were mapped to department = 'HR' so the filter still matches it
Whether the foundation model's context window is large enough for the document
Whether the guardrail's denied topics configuration is blocking the response
Whether Provisioned Throughput is provisioned for the embedding model
explanation: A metadata filter that does not match a migrated document's attributes silently excludes it from the retrieval candidate set even though the file exists and is chunked correctly, so the fix is to verify the migrated metadata still satisfies department = 'HR'. Context window size and Provisioned Throughput affect the model call, not which chunks Retrieve returns, and a guardrail denied-topics block would produce a visibly blocked response rather than a silent retrieval miss.

stem: A team instruments a RAG chatbot with timers around retrieval, a custom re-ranking step, and the Bedrock model call, then compares the results to the Bedrock InvocationLatency metric. They find that the model call accounts for only about 15 percent of total response time, while re-ranking and orchestration account for the rest. Leadership proposes purchasing Provisioned Throughput for the foundation model to fix the latency complaint. How should the team respond?
options: Agree, because Provisioned Throughput eliminates cold-start latency for every stage of the pipeline
Push back, because Provisioned Throughput only reduces the model call's latency, and the measurements show the model call is not the bottleneck
Agree, because Provisioned Throughput automatically parallelizes the re-ranking and orchestration steps
Push back, because Provisioned Throughput requires a minimum 30-day commitment regardless of workload
explanation: Provisioned Throughput only speeds up the model invocation itself; since the team's own measurements show the model call is just 15 percent of total latency, purchasing it would not meaningfully reduce the response time users experience. It does not touch the re-ranking or orchestration code and does not parallelize custom pipeline steps. The commitment claim is also wrong on its own terms: Provisioned Throughput offers a no-commitment option alongside 1-month and 6-month terms, so there is no mandatory 30-day minimum - and the commitment length would not be the reason to reject this proposal anyway.

stem: A platform team is writing internal debugging guidelines for engineers who support a Bedrock-based agentic RAG system. Select the TWO statements that are correct.
options: CloudTrail is the best source for viewing an AgentCore agent's step-by-step reasoning and the inputs and outputs of each tool it invoked
A metadata filter that does not match a document's indexed attributes can silently exclude that document from Retrieve results, even though the document exists in the knowledge base
Provisioned Throughput reduces end-to-end response latency regardless of which pipeline stage is the actual bottleneck
Switching to a larger foundation model generally increases response latency rather than reducing it
When the correct passage is missing from Retrieve results, the issue should first be treated as a generation problem and fixed by editing the prompt template
explanation: A mismatched metadata filter can silently drop an existing, correctly chunked document from Retrieve results, and larger models are usually slower, not faster, so switching model size can worsen latency. CloudTrail records API activity, not an agent's reasoning trace (that is AgentCore Observability's job); Provisioned Throughput only helps when the model call itself is the bottleneck; and a missing passage that exists in the knowledge base is a retrieval fault, not a generation fault, so it should not be diagnosed by editing the prompt.

stem: A team configures a CloudWatch alarm on the Amazon Bedrock InvocationLatency metric using the Average statistic. The alarm has never fired even though a growing share of user requests are visibly slow. What is the MOST likely reason the alarm is failing to catch this, and how should the team fix it?
options: The Average statistic smooths out the slow tail; the team should change the alarm to evaluate a percentile statistic such as p90 or p99 instead
CloudWatch alarms cannot be configured on InvocationLatency at all, so the team must switch to model invocation logging
The alarm threshold is too low; the team should raise it until it stops firing spuriously
Latency alarms require AWS CloudTrail data events to be enabled first, or they will never trigger
explanation: A plain average can mask a slow tail that a real share of users experience, so the alarm should evaluate a percentile statistic (p90/p99) on InvocationLatency rather than the Average. CloudWatch does support alarms on InvocationLatency, raising the threshold would make the alarm even less sensitive to the real problem, and CloudTrail data events have no bearing on whether a CloudWatch alarm can trigger.

stem: A regulated healthcare company deploying an Amazon Bedrock-based clinical-summary assistant must be able to (1) regenerate the exact same output from the exact same input when an auditor reruns a historical case, and (2) retrieve the verbatim prompt and completion that were sent and returned for any past production request. Which two actions together satisfy both requirements? (Choose 2.)
options: Set temperature to 0 and constrain top-p and top-k for effectively deterministic decoding
Enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 and/or CloudWatch Logs
Enable AWS CloudTrail logging for the Bedrock API
Configure CloudWatch alarms on InvocationLatency and InvocationServerErrors
Increase the model's maximum output token limit
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0668 for current practice. Supported low-variability settings can make diagnostic comparisons more stable, but cannot guarantee exact regeneration. Protected invocation logging captures supported request and response payloads so an auditor can inspect the original text. Pin versions and record configuration; replay the stored original when exact historical wording is needed.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Resolve the source-audited accuracy issue without changing a published answer key.

stem: A team's operations dashboard reports that average InvocationLatency for a production Bedrock application is well within the target SLA. Despite this, a growing number of users complain that responses occasionally take far too long. Which change to the monitoring approach would BEST explain and surface this discrepancy?
options: Track latency using percentiles such as p90 and p99 instead of the mean, since a small number of slow requests can be hidden by an otherwise healthy average
Switch the alarm's statistic from Sum to SampleCount so every invocation is individually counted
Reduce the CloudWatch alarm evaluation period from 5 minutes to 1 minute so spikes are detected faster
Replace the InvocationLatency metric with InvocationServerErrors, since the complaints are actually caused by throttling errors
explanation: Averages hide a slow tail; tracking p90/p99 percentiles surfaces the subset of requests that are actually slow even when the mean looks healthy. Changing the statistic to SampleCount, shortening the evaluation period, or swapping to an error-count metric do not address the mean-versus-tail-latency gap described.

stem: A team is finalizing its testing and observability standards for a production Amazon Bedrock application. During review, two engineers make competing claims about the platform's built-in capabilities. Which two of the following claims are TECHNICALLY CORRECT? (Choose two.)
options: Setting temperature to 0 and constraining top-p and top-k produces deterministic, reproducible completions for the same input
Tracking only the average value of InvocationLatency is sufficient because it always reflects what slow-tail users experience
A CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationServerErrors metric can trigger an automated notification when server-side error rates rise
AWS CloudTrail records the full prompt and completion text for every InvokeModel call, making Model invocation logging unnecessary
Retrying a failing regression test until it passes is an acceptable way to resolve nondeterministic evaluation failures
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0669 for current practice. Lower supported sampling settings can reduce variability without ensuring identical responses. CloudWatch alarms can notify on the configured server-error metric. Averages can hide tail latency, CloudTrail is not a full inference-payload archive, and retrying tests until they pass conceals instability.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Resolve the source-audited accuracy issue without changing a published answer key.

stem: A localization team has professionally translated reference sentences for 10,000 source strings in a new documentation-translation feature built on an Amazon Bedrock model. They want a fast, quantifiable overlap score against those references without involving any reviewers. Which Amazon Bedrock evaluation job type is MOST appropriate?
options: An automatic evaluation job using reference-based metrics such as BERTScore and F1
An LLM-as-a-judge evaluation job scoring coherence and tone
A human evaluation job routing translations to bilingual subject-matter experts
A canary rollout comparing the new translation prompt against the current version
explanation: Automatic (reference-based) metrics like BERTScore and F1 are built for exactly this case: gold reference outputs already exist and the team wants a fast, repeatable overlap score. An LLM-as-a-judge job is unnecessary since no nuanced, reference-free judgment is required, human evaluation is too slow for 10,000 strings, and a canary rollout tests production traffic, not a one-time overlap score.

stem: An internal HR chatbot answers free-form employee questions about benefits and policy. A team wants to automatically score helpfulness, tone, and conciseness across about 8,000 conversation transcripts every night with no human reviewers involved, and no single correct wording exists for any answer. Which Amazon Bedrock evaluation job type is MOST appropriate?
options: An automatic evaluation job using reference-based metrics such as F1
An LLM-as-a-judge evaluation job scoring the team's own prompt dataset against the defined quality dimensions
A human evaluation job with subject-matter expert reviewers
Amazon Bedrock Prompt management to version the system prompt
explanation: LLM-as-a-judge is built for automatic, nightly scoring of nuanced dimensions like helpfulness and tone at scale using the team's own prompts, with no gold references needed. Reference-based metrics cannot work without a single correct answer, human review cannot scale to 8,000 transcripts nightly, and Prompt management only stores and versions prompts, it does not score quality.

stem: An insurance company generates claim-denial explanation letters with a Bedrock model. Once per quarter, licensed claims adjusters must review a curated sample of 50 letters and certify that the language meets state fair-claims-handling regulations before the sample is submitted to a regulator. Which Amazon Bedrock evaluation job type is MOST appropriate for this quarterly certification?
options: An automatic evaluation job using reference-based metrics
An LLM-as-a-judge evaluation job running on every generated letter
A human evaluation job routing the sample to the company's own subject-matter experts
A canary rollout comparing denial-letter quality against the prior model version
explanation: Human evaluation is reserved for subjective, high-stakes sign-off where mistakes carry regulatory weight and a judge model is not authoritative enough, exactly this quarterly certification by licensed adjusters. Reference-based metrics need gold outputs that do not exist for unique denial letters, LLM-as-a-judge is for automatic scoring at release scale rather than regulator-facing certification, and a canary rollout measures live traffic quality, not a compliance sign-off on a fixed sample.

stem: A marketing team generates a uniquely personalized newsletter summary for every subscriber, so there is no single correct reference text for any given output. They want an automatic, repeatable quality gate they can run before every send. Which evaluation job type is LEAST suitable here, and why?
options: Automatic (reference-based) metrics, because they require gold reference outputs that do not exist for uniquely personalized text
LLM-as-a-judge, because it cannot run automatically on every release
Human evaluation, because it is the fastest way to gate every send
Automatic (reference-based) metrics, because they cannot be run repeatedly on a schedule
explanation: Automatic reference-based metrics need gold reference outputs to compute overlap, and uniquely personalized newsletter text has no such reference, which is why the method is unsuitable here. LLM-as-a-judge is well suited to automatic, repeatable scoring so option B's reasoning is false, human evaluation is the slowest option rather than the fastest so option C's reasoning is false, and reference-based metrics are otherwise perfectly repeatable so option D's reasoning is also false.

stem: A team is choosing an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job type and is told that one option is generally the most accurate at capturing true response quality, but is too slow and costly to run on every release. Which evaluation job type are they describing?
options: Automatic (reference-based) metrics
LLM-as-a-judge
Human evaluation
Canary or A/B rollout
explanation: Human evaluation routes responses to subject-matter experts and is the most accurate approach, but it is reserved for infrequent, high-stakes sign-off rather than every release because of its speed and cost. Automatic metrics and LLM-as-a-judge are both designed to run cheaply and repeatedly, and a canary rollout is a traffic-routing strategy, not an evaluation-scoring method.

stem: A content-moderation team auto-generates explanation messages describing why a post was flagged. Volume is about 4,000 messages per day, mistakes are annoying but not high-stakes or regulated, and the team needs a fully automatic score computed every day. A colleague suggests routing every message to human reviewers instead, arguing human judgment is always more trustworthy. Why is this the wrong choice here?
options: Human evaluation cannot scale to this daily volume and is reserved for infrequent, high-stakes review, while an LLM-as-a-judge job can score nuanced dimensions automatically at this scale
Human evaluation requires gold reference outputs that do not exist for these messages
Human evaluation only supports comparing two candidate models side by side, not scoring a single model's output
Human evaluation cannot measure nuanced dimensions like tone or clarity at all
explanation: Human evaluation is the most accurate option but is too slow and costly to repeat at high daily volume, so it should be reserved for infrequent, high-stakes sign-off, while an LLM-as-a-judge job is built to score nuanced dimensions automatically at this scale. Human evaluation does not require gold references, that describes reference-based metrics, it is not limited to comparing two models, and it can absolutely judge nuanced dimensions, its limitation here is scale and cost, not capability.

stem: A team has a small, high-quality dataset of 200 gold reference responses for a technical-support assistant. They now want to score how empathetic and easy to follow each new response is, dimensions their gold references do not explicitly encode. Which evaluation job type is MOST appropriate, even though gold references are available?
options: Automatic (reference-based) metrics, since gold references already exist
LLM-as-a-judge, scoring empathy and clarity against the team's own criteria
Human evaluation, since gold references make automatic scoring unnecessary
A canary rollout comparing the new prompt to the prior version
explanation: Automatic reference-based metrics are the wrong choice whenever quality is nuanced, even if gold references happen to exist, because they measure surface overlap and cannot capture dimensions like empathy; an LLM-as-a-judge job scores exactly these nuanced dimensions at scale. Having references does not make automatic metrics the right tool here, human evaluation is reserved for high-stakes sign-off rather than routine nuanced scoring, and a canary rollout tests live traffic, not offline response quality.

stem: A marketing operations team uses a generative AI model to draft thousands of product description variants every day. Before each batch goes live, they need an automated score for tone consistency and coherence across every generated description, without any manual review step. Which Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job type is MOST appropriate?
options: Automatic (reference-based) metrics such as BERTScore or F1
LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
Human evaluation by subject matter experts
CloudWatch alarms on InvocationLatency
explanation: BERTScore uses contextual BERT embeddings and cosine similarity to measure semantic similarity against reference text; it is not just lexical overlap. That score alone does not establish factual faithfulness, coherence, empathy or brand tone. Choose a rubric-based judge or human review where those dimensions matter, and calibrate the evaluation on representative cases. The scenario explicitly requires unattended scoring for all descriptions, so a rubric-based LLM judge fits the automation requirement; latency alarms do not score quality.

stem: A bank's generative AI assistant drafts plain-language explanations of loan decisions for customers. Before the quarterly compliance release, the legal and compliance team insists on manually reviewing a sample of the explanations for regulatory tone and fairness, because a mistake here carries regulatory risk that no automated scorer can be trusted to catch. Which evaluation job type should gate this quarterly sign-off?
options: Automatic (reference-based) metrics like BERTScore
LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
Human evaluation by subject matter experts
Provisioned Throughput load testing
explanation: Human evaluation is reserved for subjective, high-stakes sign-off where mistakes carry regulatory or legal weight and a judge model is not authoritative enough. Automatic metrics and LLM-as-a-judge are built for frequent, automated scoring rather than a one-time high-stakes legal sign-off, and Provisioned Throughput testing addresses capacity, not response quality.

stem: A localization team maintains a benchmark dataset of source sentences paired with verified correct translations. After every fine-tuning run, they need a fast, low-cost, repeatable numeric score to detect translation quality regressions, and a gold-standard translation already exists for every input. Which evaluation job type fits this need?
options: Human evaluation by bilingual reviewers
LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
Automatic (reference-based) metrics such as BERTScore or F1
AgentCore Observability tracing
explanation: With verified reference translations, an automatic semantic/reference metric such as BERTScore provides a repeatable regression signal. BERTScore compares contextual embeddings rather than only lexical surface overlap. Reference scores do not eliminate the value of separate human or judge-based checks for meaning, fluency and task-specific errors.

stem: An HR technology company is rolling out a generative AI assistant that answers employee questions about workplace conduct policy company-wide. Before the rollout, HR and legal stakeholders insist on reviewing a sample of the assistant's responses themselves, since a poorly worded answer here creates reputational and legal exposure they do not trust any automated scorer to catch. Which evaluation job type should be used for this pre-rollout review?
options: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
Automatic (reference-based) metrics
Human evaluation
A CI gate on a golden dataset with an automated pass/fail threshold
explanation: Human evaluation routes responses to subject matter experts and is the right choice for subjective, high-stakes sign-off where mistakes carry legal or reputational risk. LLM-as-a-judge and automatic metrics scale well for frequent, automated scoring but are not considered authoritative enough for this kind of sign-off, and a CI gate on a golden dataset measures regression against a fixed threshold, not subjective legal risk.

stem: A platform team wants to add an evaluation step to their CI/CD pipeline so that every pull request touching the system prompt of a customer support assistant is automatically scored, within minutes, for coherence and faithfulness across a dataset of several thousand prompts, with no manual review in the loop. Which evaluation job type should they configure the pipeline to run?
options: Human evaluation with a sample review queue
Automatic (reference-based) metrics such as F1
LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using a custom prompt dataset
Provisioned Throughput failover testing
explanation: LLM-as-a-judge is built for automatically scoring nuanced dimensions like coherence and faithfulness across large datasets on every release, exactly matching this pipeline's requirement. Human evaluation cannot run unattended in a CI pipeline, reference-based metrics do not capture coherence or faithfulness well, and Provisioned Throughput testing checks capacity, not quality.

stem: Which Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job type requires the team to supply gold-standard reference outputs and scores generated responses by measuring surface-level overlap with those references, using metrics such as BERTScore or F1?
options: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
Human evaluation
Automatic (reference-based) metrics
AgentCore Observability
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0670 for current practice. Reference-based BERTScore uses contextual embedding similarity, whereas F1 compares predicted and reference token/label overlap according to the selected task. These metrics require reference data for the stated comparison and are not comprehensive proof of factual faithfulness, coherence or tone.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Resolve the source-audited accuracy issue without changing a published answer key.

stem: A developer runs an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG evaluation job for a customer-support assistant. One of the reported scores is described as measuring whether the passages the retriever pulled back are topically relevant to the user's question, independent of what the model ultimately generates. Which metric is being described?
options: Context relevance
Faithfulness
Correctness
End-to-end latency
explanation: Context relevance isolates retrieval quality by scoring whether the retrieved passages are on topic, separate from the generated answer. Faithfulness scores whether the answer avoids introducing claims not grounded in those passages (a generation-side check), Correctness scores whether the answer accurately answers the question, and latency is not a RAG evaluation quality metric.

stem: A RAG evaluation job for a legal-research assistant reports low scores across context relevance, faithfulness, and correctness for the same batch of test questions. Which explanation BEST accounts for all three scores degrading together?
options: The foundation model has a hallucination bug that also happens to suppress the context relevance score.
Retrieval is failing to surface on-topic passages, and the poor faithfulness and correctness scores are a downstream consequence of the model having nothing accurate to work with.
The evaluation job's LLM judge is miscalibrated and uniformly under-scores every dimension.
A guardrail's contextual grounding check is silently blocking every response before scoring.
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0671 for current practice. Here independent inspection confirms an off-topic retrieval result, so retrieval failure is supported by evidence rather than inferred solely from judge scores. Poor retrieved context can contribute to poor answer quality, but low judge-scored metrics alone do not rule out evaluator miscalibration. Verify the retrieved passages and evaluator before assigning a cause.
exclusionReason: Replaced after source review: Resolve the source-audited accuracy issue without changing a published answer key.

stem: A new engineer is triaging a Knowledge Bases RAG evaluation report and needs to identify which score would have caught the model inventing a claim that is not present anywhere in the retrieved passages. Which metric correctly captures this failure?
options: Faithfulness
Context relevance
Correctness
End-to-end latency
explanation: Faithfulness measures whether the response avoids introducing claims that are not grounded in the retrieved text chunks, catching exactly this kind of model-added, invented content. The other options describe different dimensions: topical fit of retrieved passages is context relevance, whether the answer accurately answers the question is correctness, and pipeline speed is latency, none of which detect an invented claim.

stem: A RAG evaluation job repeatedly shows low faithfulness for a medical-information assistant. The team wants to stop ungrounded answers from ever reaching end users in production, not just measure the problem after the fact. Which Amazon Bedrock capability should they configure?
options: Model invocation logging to capture every prompt and completion for later audit.
A Bedrock guardrail with the contextual grounding check enabled, with grounding and relevance thresholds set to block unsupported responses.
A higher top-k value on the knowledge base retrieval configuration.
Bedrock Prompt management to version and store the system prompt.
explanation: The contextual grounding check in Bedrock guardrails scores grounding and relevance at inference time and can block a response before it reaches the user when either score falls below its configured threshold. Invocation logging and Prompt management only record and store data without blocking a response, and a higher top-k changes what is retrieved but does not gate on grounding or relevance.

stem: Two candidate RAG configurations are evaluated with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG evaluation on the same question set. Configuration A: context relevance 0.55, faithfulness 0.94, correctness 0.52. Configuration B: context relevance 0.90, faithfulness 0.91, correctness 0.88. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Configuration A is better because it has the highest faithfulness score.
The two configurations are equivalent because faithfulness is the only score that matters for a RAG system.
Configuration A is better because a model that never adds unsupported content is always safer for production regardless of the other scores.

Configuration B is better overall: its retrieval is far stronger, and its answers stay faithful to the source while also correctly answering the question, whereas Configuration A's low context relevance and correctness show it usually fails to retrieve or use the right information even though it rarely fabricates content.
explanation: Archived question: The published question required correction. Use aipc01-0672 for current practice. Configuration B has much better Context relevance (0.90 versus 0.55) and Correctness (0.88 versus 0.52), with a small decrease in Faithfulness (0.91 versus 0.94).
