The condition key is present for foundation-model evaluation, but not for the profile resource evaluation, so applying that condition indiscriminately to both can deny the intended call. With no other applicable invocation grants, direct model invocation is not allowed.

stem: A platform team allows developers across the organization to invoke an approved list of foundation models, but wants to prevent any member account from starting an unauthorized fine-tuning (model customization) job outside a single, vetted ML platform member account, with the LEAST ongoing administrative effort. What should they do?
options: Ask each account owner to avoid starting customization jobs unless authorized.
Rely on the existing model-invocation SCP from the InvokeModel restriction, since it also covers customization jobs.
Delete the IAM permissions for bedrock:InvokeModel in every account except the ML platform account.
Attach an AWS Organizations service control policy that denies bedrock:CreateModelCustomizationJob in member accounts except the vetted ML platform account.
explanation: An SCP denying bedrock:CreateModelCustomizationJob outside the approved platform member account provides centralized preventive enforcement for member-account principals. An InvokeModel restriction does not cover customization-job creation. SCPs do not restrict the management account, whose access needs separate controls.

stem: A workload uses a Bedrock interface VPC endpoint and IAM permissions for approved models. Security requires two additional controls: restrict what can pass through that endpoint, and prevent the application role from invoking Bedrock through a public endpoint even if it later receives a broad Allow policy. Which design meets both requirements?
options: Use a custom endpoint policy for allowed principals/actions/resources, plus an explicitly enforced IAM Deny on the role's Bedrock invocation actions when aws:SourceVpce does not match the approved endpoint.
Use only the interface endpoint's default full-access policy.
Use only a custom endpoint policy; it also controls calls sent directly to public Bedrock endpoints.
Enable S3 Block Public Access on the application's data bucket.
explanation: An endpoint policy limits requests that traverse that endpoint. A separate explicit Deny using aws:SourceVpce prevents the application role from bypassing it through another route; cover both InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream for ordinary and streamed inference. Ensure administrators cannot remove the required controls. Endpoint policies alone do not govern public-endpoint calls.

stem: An AgentCore application needs to create a Memory resource encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Which configuration follows the documented permissions approach?
options: Use only an S3 bucket policy; Memory does not use AWS KMS permissions.
Assume a customer-managed key is used automatically without configuration.

Specify the KMS key when creating Memory and authorize the setup IAM user or role for required KMS operations, including CreateGrant, Decrypt, DescribeKey, data-key generation and ReEncrypt, scoped with kms:ViaService for AgentCore.
Grant the Memory resource public access so any principal can decrypt it.
explanation: AgentCore Memory supports a customer-managed KMS key. The encryption guide shows permissions attached to the setup IAM user or role, including CreateGrant, Decrypt, DescribeKey, GenerateDataKey, GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext and ReEncrypt*, with a kms:ViaService condition. Ensure the KMS key policy also permits the relevant identity's use. A bucket policy is not a substitute for KMS authorization.

stem: Users upload documents into an S3 data source for a Bedrock knowledge base. The team wants to screen each parsed document for harmful content before creating its custom chunks and indexing them. It will implement the chunking logic itself. Which ingestion configuration fits?
options: Set chunkingStrategy to NONE and configure a custom transformation Lambda at the supported POST_CHUNKING hook; screen the parsed document with ApplyGuardrail, return only approved content as custom chunks, and fail closed on rejected content.
Select fixed-size chunking and assume the transformation Lambda always runs before Bedrock chunks the documents.
Rely only on the guardrail applied to the final generated response.
Ask uploaders to self-certify that their documents are appropriate.
explanation: The custom transformation hook is POST_CHUNKING. Selecting NONE leaves parsed content available for Lambda to screen and custom-chunk before returning approved chunks for downstream processing. With a native chunking strategy, Lambda receives already-chunked content. The transformation must omit rejected content or fail the workflow; merely flagging it while returning it would not prevent indexing.

stem: A supported Bedrock model offers Priority, Flex, and Standard service tiers through the runtime API. A team wants low-latency prioritization for live chat, discounted processing with longer response times for delay-tolerant synchronous summaries, and ordinary Standard service for routine text generation. It is not reserving capacity. Which service_tier values match those workloads, in that order?
options: "priority", "flex", "default"
"reserved", "reserved", "reserved"
"flex", "priority", "default"
"priority", "flex", "standard"
explanation: Priority prioritizes requests at a premium; Flex trades longer processing time for a discount. Standard is selected by omitting the parameter or using "default". The literal value "standard" is not a supported service_tier value. Reserved requires a separate reservation.

stem: A team uses explicit prompt caching with Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Bedrock. Its entire prefix before the only cache checkpoint, counting all preceding fields, is 600 tokens. Calls use the same model endpoint and Region and recur within the TTL, but the prefix never produces cache reads. What documented limitation explains this?
options: Claude models do not support explicit prompt caching.
The 600-token cumulative prefix is below this model's 1,024-token minimum for an explicit cache checkpoint.
Explicit caching requires Provisioned Throughput.
Every repeated prefix is cached regardless of its length.
explanation: Claude Sonnet 4.5 has a documented 1,024-token minimum for explicit caching. A shorter total prefix is not cached even when the request succeeds. The minimum applies to the cumulative prefix before the checkpoint. A qualifying length makes content eligible; it does not guarantee a hit.

stem: A team wants a forecast-based warning before monthly Bedrock spend exceeds its target and an automatic policy restriction after AWS billing data shows actual spend crossing a threshold. It accepts billing-data delay and understands this does not guarantee an exact hard spending cap. Which TWO capabilities should it configure? (Select TWO.)
options: An AWS Budgets forecasted-spend alert below the monthly target.
GuardDuty configured to stop Bedrock billing at a dollar threshold.
A latency dashboard that blocks model invocations automatically.
A Bedrock Guardrail with a dollar-denial policy.
An AWS Budgets action configured for automatic execution that applies a restrictive IAM policy or SCP when the actual-spend threshold is detected.
explanation: Budget alerts support forecast warnings, and Budget actions can apply restrictive policies automatically when evaluated thresholds are exceeded. Billing updates and notifications are delayed, so spend can overshoot before the restriction takes effect. These controls do not provide an exact hard cap. The other services do not implement the stated billing controls.

stem: A RAG assistant returns fluent but wrong answers. For the failing cases, the developer has verified that Retrieve returns the correct answer passages and that those passages are included, untruncated, in the generator input. Which evaluation signals should the developer inspect next?
options: Generation metrics, particularly faithfulness and correctness, because the required evidence has been verified in the actual generator context but the answer still misuses it.
The retrieval metrics, because a well-written but wrong answer always means the wrong documents were retrieved.
Neither family is relevant to a "wrong answer" symptom; only latency metrics matter.
Only context coverage matters, since it alone determines whether an answer can ever be correct.
explanation: A source document being ingested does not prove its answer passage was retrieved. In this revised scenario, the developer has independently confirmed that the correct passages were retrieved and included in the generator input, so generation correctness and faithfulness are the appropriate next checks. Without that confirmation, inspect retrieval first.

stem: An on-call engineer sees AccessDeniedException, ThrottlingException, ValidationException and ServiceQuotaExceededException from different Bedrock runtime requests. Which pairing is CORRECT?
options: AccessDeniedException means the account exceeded its requests-per-minute limit for the model.
ValidationException means the model has not been granted access in Bedrock model access settings.
ServiceQuotaExceededException, in this context, means the prompt payload exceeded the model's maximum input size.
ThrottlingException means the request rate is currently exceeding the account's per-model throughput limit, independent of any quota-increase request.
explanation: ThrottlingException is a runtime quota/rate-limit signal. AccessDeniedException concerns authorization/access, and ValidationException concerns request constraints. ServiceQuotaExceededException on InvokeModel means the request exceeds the account service quota; it does not describe AWS refusing a request to raise that quota.

stem: A team no longer needs its Bedrock Provisioned Throughput after the commitment term ends. The base model supports on-demand invocation, which better fits the new sporadic traffic. The application currently uses the provisioned model ARN as modelId. Which migration is appropriate?
options: Update and validate the application to use the supported on-demand model ID or inference profile, then delete the now-deletable Provisioned Throughput to stop its capacity charges.
Delete Provisioned Throughput and keep invoking its deleted ARN, relying on automatic on-demand fallback.
Renew a six-month commitment before testing on-demand access.
Convert the base model to a custom model to restore on-demand eligibility.
explanation: Provisioned inference is targeted using the provisioned model ARN. Moving to on-demand requires changing the invocation target; deleting that ARN does not supply automatic fallback. After migration and once deletion is permitted, delete the provisioned capacity because billing continues until deletion.

stem: A knowledge management team wants a straightforward Bedrock Knowledge Bases chunking configuration that lets them set a maximum token count per chunk and an overlap percentage, without enabling semantic boundary detection or parent/child levels. Which strategy matches?
options: Fixed-size chunking
Hierarchical chunking
Semantic chunking
No chunking
explanation: Fixed-size chunking is configured with a token limit and overlap percentage. Hierarchical chunking adds parent and child sizes; semantic chunking uses sentence relationships and a breakpoint threshold; no chunking treats the document as one chunk. A token limit does not imply that all document boundaries are ignored: Bedrock can preserve logical boundaries for parsed content.

stem: A home-goods retailer wants image-to-image similarity search: it will embed catalog photos and uploaded customer photos with the same Bedrock model. Which listed model natively supports image embeddings for this purpose?
options: Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2
Cohere Embed v3 Multilingual
Amazon Nova Micro
Amazon Rerank
explanation: Cohere Embed v3 Multilingual supports image embeddings on Bedrock. It can encode the catalog and query photos for similarity search. The capability comes from its documented multimodal image support, not merely from multilingual text support. Titan Text Embeddings V2 is text-only, Nova Micro generates text, and Amazon Rerank scores retrieved text relevance instead of producing image embeddings.

stem: A team has raw customer-service emails but no examples of ideal support replies. They want to use Amazon Bedrock supervised fine-tuning to teach the model their response style. What should they do before starting the job?
options: Submit the raw emails and let supervised fine-tuning invent the target replies automatically.
Curate representative inputs with reviewed target replies, then serialize those examples as JSONL using the selected model's required record schema.
Put the emails in a Bedrock Guardrail so the guardrail updates the model weights.
Build a Knowledge Base and treat retrieval as a completed supervised fine-tuning job.
explanation: Supervised fine-tuning needs examples that demonstrate the desired response. Curate input/output examples and follow the selected model's JSONL schema; it may use prompt/completion fields or conversational messages. Raw emails alone do not supply reviewed target replies. Guardrails and retrieval do not perform supervised model training.

stem: An AgentCore Gateway exposes a read-only get_order_status tool and an update_order tool needed by other agents. A support agent must be prevented from calling update_order even if prompted to do so. Which control best enforces this at the Gateway boundary?
options: Associate a Policy in AgentCore engine with the Gateway and configure formal authorization policies that permit this agent only the read-only tool.
Add a system prompt saying that the agent should never modify orders.
Use a Bedrock Guardrail to rewrite the model's text after the update tool has executed.
Store a reminder of the read-only requirement in short-term memory.
explanation: Policy in AgentCore evaluates requests at the Gateway boundary against configured formal policies. Policies can be written in Cedar or authored through natural language that generates and validates policy code; deterministic enforcement does not mean interpreting raw English rules on each call. Bind the policy to the correct agent identity and tool, and validate its decisions. Prompt instructions, output filtering, and memory do not enforce tool authorization.

stem: A fintech team uses a Bedrock Converse model that supports structured outputs. Setting temperature to 0 still allows commentary before an extracted receipt JSON object. Which explanation and change BEST address the formatting problem?
options: Increase temperature; higher randomness enforces JSON syntax.
Lower topP and assume the output will match any required schema.
Claude on Bedrock has no schema-constrained output capability, so a regex is the only solution.
Temperature controls sampling rather than the output contract; configure a supported JSON Schema through outputConfig.textFormat.
explanation: Structured outputs enforce a supported JSON Schema; temperature does not. Using outputConfig.textFormat on a supported Converse model addresses the requested response structure. Sampling settings do not enforce property names or types. Handle API errors and incomplete responses, and separately validate business facts such as receipt totals.

stem: A security review of a large AWS Organization finds that a developer holding full IAM administrative permissions in one member account wrote an inline policy granting their own role bedrock:InvokeModel on a foundation model that is not on the organization's approved list, and successfully invoked it. Leadership wants a single, central control that blocks this even when a member account's own administrator misconfigures or bypasses that account's IAM policies. Which control blocks both synchronous and streamed inference on unapproved models in member accounts?
options: An identity-based IAM policy attached to every role in every account that lists the approved models
An AWS Organizations service control policy (SCP), attached at the OU or organization root, that denies both InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream for every model ARN except the approved ones
An IAM permissions boundary attached only to that one developer's role
A Bedrock guardrail with a denied-topics policy applied to the model
explanation: An SCP attached to the relevant OU centrally limits permissions for member-account principals, including account administrators, and is inherited by accounts placed there. Deny both InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream on unapproved model resources to cover synchronous and streamed inference, including their Converse equivalents. An SCP does not grant permissions and does not restrict the organization's management-account principals. Content guardrails do not enforce a model allowlist.

stem: Teams A and B share an AgentCore Gateway. Team A may call shipping-status tools; only Team B may call refund tools. The Gateway's service role legitimately needs permission to invoke both backends. Security wants Team A's caller identity to be unable to invoke refund tools even after prompt injection. What is the MOST direct control?
options: Keep both tools available and rely only on the model's system instructions.
Add a denied topic blocking messages containing the word refund.
Log calls and investigate cross-team access after execution.
Attach and enforce AgentCore Policy authorization at the Gateway that permits each authenticated team identity to call only its approved tools and denies Team A's refund calls.
explanation: The missing boundary is caller-to-tool authorization. An enforced AgentCore Policy evaluates access at the Gateway before tool execution, preventing Team A from calling refund even though the Gateway service role can invoke that backend. Separate least-privilege backend roles remain useful but do not by themselves decide which Gateway caller may reach each tool.

stem: A platform team governs Bedrock synchronous and streamed inference in AWS Organizations member accounts. The team controls policy administration so application developers cannot remove required policies. It needs (1) an approved-model allowlist regardless of additional IAM Allow grants, and (2) every allowed invocation to specify an approved guardrail. Which TWO controls together satisfy this? (Select TWO.)
options: An AWS Organizations SCP that denies both bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream for unapproved model resource ARNs in member accounts.

An IAM policy statement, attached to the roles that call Bedrock, that denies bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream unless the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key matches the approved guardrail.
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging delivered to an S3 bucket for later review.
A resource-based policy attached to each approved foundation model listing the accounts allowed to invoke it.
AWS CloudTrail with a metric filter and alarm on InvokeModel calls that omit a guardrail.
explanation: The SCP must deny both InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream for unapproved models; denying only InvokeModel leaves streaming access uncovered. A protected explicit Deny using bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier on both actions enforces the approved guardrail. Both operate at request authorization time. SCPs restrict member-account permissions; they do not cover management-account principals or grant access.

stem: An audit team receives unmodified images generated by Amazon Titan Image Generator. It wants to check two provenance signals that Titan attaches at generation time, while recognizing that later edits can reduce watermark detection accuracy or remove metadata. Which TWO signals should it inspect? (Select TWO.)
options: Bedrock watermark detection to recover the invisible watermark embedded by Titan Image Generator
C2PA Content Credentials
A SHA-256 hash captured at generation time
A visible watermark or logo added by the application
EXIF metadata tags added by the application
explanation: Titan adds an invisible watermark and C2PA metadata to generated images. Watermark detection checks for the embedded watermark; Content Credentials can show signed generation provenance when the metadata remains present. These are useful provenance signals, not an unconditional guarantee after modification: AWS warns that edits can reduce watermark detection accuracy, and metadata can be removed. Application-added hashes, logos, or ordinary EXIF tags are not these built-in signals.

stem: An existing SageMaker Clarify customer runs a credit-scoring model on a SageMaker AI inference endpoint with structured applicant features. It needs per-record feature attributions for an audit. Which capability fits?
options: Raise the guardrail's contextual grounding check threshold
Amazon SageMaker Clarify explainability reports
Bedrock model invocation logging
AWS Artifact
explanation: For existing customers, Clarify's model-agnostic SHAP analysis can produce local feature attributions for individual predictions on a supported SageMaker AI endpoint. This is distinct from content filtering, request logging, and AWS infrastructure attestations. Clarify is closed to new customers; AWS publishes migration guidance including standardized bias metrics and SHAP-based solutions.

stem: A support assistant attaches a Bedrock guardrail to InvokeModel, but its denied-topic policy has input evaluation disabled and output blocking enabled. Many user requests explicitly ask for denied topics, and their generated responses are blocked after paid inference. The team wants an explicit application gate before invoking the model. Which change meets that goal?
options: Enable the denied-topic policy's input evaluation and call ApplyGuardrail on the user message; invoke the model only if that check allows it.
Remove the guardrail and rely on a system prompt to refuse denied topics.
Switch tiers while leaving input checks disabled and expect all denied inputs to be rejected before generation.
Use a post-response word filter while leaving input evaluation disabled.
explanation: Enable input evaluation for the denied-topic policy and call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT before invoking the model; reject requests it blocks. This adds the requested application gate. An attached guardrail with equivalent input blocking enabled already avoids model-inference charges when it blocks the input, so this is not a general cost advantage over correctly configured attached input filtering. Output-side interventions occur after paid generation.

stem: A company regularly acquires smaller businesses, and each acquisition's AWS member accounts are moved into the parent AWS Organization within days of closing. The security team wants the newly onboarded accounts restricted to a pre-approved list of Bedrock foundation models from the moment they land in the Organization, without any manual policy work on a per-account basis. Which approach covers both synchronous and streamed inference?
options: Ask each acquired company's cloud team to attach an identical IAM policy to every role that calls Bedrock in their accounts.
Configure an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topics policy and require every new account to reference it.

Attach an AWS Organizations service control policy at the relevant organizational unit that denies both bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream for every model ARN except the approved list, so it is inherited automatically by any account placed under that OU.
Create a shared IAM role in the management account and have every acquired account's application assume it before calling Bedrock.
explanation: An SCP attached to the relevant OU centrally limits permissions for member-account principals, including account administrators, and is inherited by accounts placed there. Deny both InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream on unapproved model resources to cover synchronous and streamed inference, including their Converse equivalents. An SCP does not grant permissions and does not restrict the organization's management-account principals. Content guardrails do not enforce a model allowlist.

stem: A telehealth startup wants to avoid creating a customer-controlled archive of Bedrock prompts and responses. It separately reviews the selected model's service-side abuse-detection retention and exceptions. Which configuration avoids creating a Bedrock model invocation log archive?
options: Enable model invocation logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs using the default log group retention setting.
Enable Amazon Macie to automatically redact prompts before they reach the model.
Leave Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging disabled.
Enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 with SSE-KMS and a narrow bucket policy.
explanation: Leaving model invocation logging disabled avoids creating prompt/response records in the customer's invocation-log destinations. It does not guarantee universal service-side zero retention: AWS documents model-specific abuse-detection rules and exceptions. Encrypted S3 or CloudWatch delivery still creates a customer archive, and Macie is not an in-flight redaction service.

stem: Users crop a platform's visible AI-generated logo from Titan images before reposting them. The platform wants to inspect Titan's built-in provenance signals, recognizing that edits can weaken detection and strip metadata. Which approach is BEST?
options: Rely only on a terms-of-service clause requiring users to preserve the logo.
Use Bedrock watermark detection and inspect C2PA Content Credentials when the metadata remains available.
Replace the small visible logo with a larger visible logo and assume cropping is impossible.
Treat a cryptographic hash of the original file as proof for every cropped or re-encoded copy.
explanation: Titan embeds an invisible watermark and attaches C2PA metadata. Watermark detection and surviving Content Credentials can provide evidence after some edits, but neither guarantees provenance for every modified image. AWS notes lower detection accuracy for modified images, and C2PA metadata can be removed. A cryptographic file hash changes when the bytes change; do not confuse this limitation with the different behavior of perceptual hashes.

stem: An organization that already used SageMaker Clarify before its new-customer availability restriction is planning continued use. Before fine-tuning a foundation model on a proprietary lending dataset, a responsible-AI team must first check whether the training data itself is statistically skewed across protected demographic groups, prior to any training run. Which AWS capability is designed for this pre-training check?
options: Configure a Bedrock guardrail's content filters at the HIGH strength setting
Amazon SageMaker Clarify to compute bias metrics on the training dataset
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to Amazon CloudWatch
Add a denied topics policy to a Bedrock guardrail
explanation: Existing Clarify customers can compute pre-training bias metrics on a structured dataset to quantify demographic skew before fitting a model. Runtime guardrails and invocation logs do not perform that analysis. Clarify is closed to new customers. AWS's migration guidance includes standardized bias metrics, SHAP, and AWS-published monitoring solutions; Bedrock Evaluations addresses foundation-model evaluation rather than every tabular bias-analysis use case.

stem: An organization that already used SageMaker Clarify before its new-customer availability restriction is planning continued use. A deployed chatbot already uses Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to block toxic language in real time. An AI risk committee now asks the team for a quantified toxicity score across a sample of the model's recent outputs to include in a quarterly governance report. What is the MOST appropriate way to produce this evidence?
options: Report the guardrail's block/allow counts as the toxicity score
Raise the guardrail's toxicity filter strength and treat the new trigger rate as the score
Run Amazon SageMaker Clarify on a sample of the model's outputs to generate a toxicity/bias report
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging and manually skim a sample of transcripts
explanation: An existing Clarify customer can use foundation-model evaluation tooling to compute a toxicity metric across sampled model outputs. Guardrail block rates measure interventions under a policy and are not equivalent to an independent toxicity metric. Clarify is already closed to new customers; AWS identifies Bedrock Evaluations as a replacement for foundation-model evaluation, including toxicity.

stem: An interactive assistant invokes Amazon Nova Pro on Bedrock through a supported on-demand API. Every request begins with the same 2,000-token instruction prefix and requests recur within the cache TTL. An engineer proposes sending user turns through the Batch inference API to reduce repeated-input cost. What is the best assessment?
options: Batch is unsuitable for the interactive response path; use prompt caching with a checkpoint after the eligible repeated prefix and monitor cache reads.
Batch is the synchronous API for cached prompts.
Provisioned Throughput is required before any prompt can be cached.
Use prompt caching within each Batch inference record because that API supports the cache-read discount.
explanation: Batch inference is asynchronous. For this supported on-demand model and eligible repeated prefix, prompt caching is the appropriate input-reuse mechanism. Successful cache reads can lower repeated-input cost and time-to-first-token; cache hits remain best effort. The Batch inference API does not support prompt caching.

stem: A Bedrock application uses a supported Claude model with a cached 5,000-token prefix and an explicit checkpoint after it. The team edits a sentence inside that prefix; no cache entry for the updated complete prefix has been created yet. Which expectation is most accurate?
options: Bedrock silently ignores the edited sentence and reuses the old complete prefix.
The edit invalidates all prompt caches in the AWS account.

The changed complete prefix cannot match the old entry. Any earlier-prefix reuse depends on eligible checkpoints or model block matching, and newly written cache tokens use the model's cache-write pricing.
Bedrock always reuses every token before the edited character and bills all remaining tokens at the standard input rate.
explanation: Cache matching depends on eligible unchanged prefixes. Editing a prefix does not produce an exact match for the old complete entry. Earlier-prefix reuse depends on the model and cache boundaries; arbitrary character-level partial reuse is not guaranteed. Cache writes can have different pricing from ordinary input, so inspect the read/write usage fields and the model pricing.

stem: An internal tool uses a supported Bedrock model at predictable high volume on weekdays and is idle at night and on weekends. For an illustrative 30-day month, its validated on-demand cost estimate is $18,000. A sufficient Provisioned Throughput allocation is quoted at $20 per hour continuously for all 720 hours, including idle periods, with no additional inference charges within that capacity. Both meet the requirements. Which cost conclusion follows from these estimates?
options: On-demand must be cheaper whenever there are any idle hours.
Provisioned Throughput costs $14,400 for the month, which is $3,600 less than the on-demand estimate despite the idle periods.
Provisioned Throughput is billed only during business hours, so its cost is lower than $14,400.
The two options must cost the same because both process the same tokens.
explanation: The stated illustrative quote gives 720 x $20 = $14,400, versus $18,000 on-demand. Fixed provisioned charges include idle hours, but idle time alone does not prove on-demand is cheaper. Use workload-specific rate and utilization estimates; these example amounts are not published AWS prices.

stem: A RAG application reduced initial retrieval from 50 candidate chunks to 5 and now misses relevant passages. It wants to keep the generation prompt limited to 5 chunks while improving selection. Which change directly addresses the lost candidates?
options: Send all 50 chunks to the generation model on every call.
Retrieve a sufficiently broad candidate set, such as 50 chunks, rerank those candidates, and pass only the 5 highest-ranked chunks to the generation model.
Rerank only the same 5 retrieved chunks and assume missing passages will be reconstructed.
Increase the generation model's temperature to recover documents that were not retrieved.
explanation: A reranker scores and reorders only the documents supplied to it. Keeping broad candidate retrieval preserves the opportunity to select relevant passages, while limiting the final reranked result count controls generation context. Reranking an already reduced set cannot recover excluded documents. Evaluate retrieval quality and include reranker charges when comparing total cost.

stem: Finance observes that the Bedrock bill for a text-generation application has tripled. Over the same period, the CloudWatch Sum of Invocations tripled, while the Average InputTokenCount and Average OutputTokenCount stayed unchanged. The model, token rates and other billed features did not change. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Average prompt size tripled, so shorten the system prompt.
Accepted request volume increased while average token size stayed stable; investigate request sources and whether the increase persists before changing capacity commitments.
The metrics prove that the number of distinct users tripled.
The unchanged token averages prove that the application cost could not have increased.
explanation: Tripled Invocations with unchanged average input and output token counts supports a request-volume explanation, assuming the model, rates and other billed features are unchanged. These metrics do not prove more distinct users or rule out retries; use request logs if that distinction matters. Monitor whether the volume persists before making capacity commitments. Larger prompts would increase average input tokens, and no model-change or latency evidence is supplied.

stem: A voice-enabled customer service bot on Amazon Bedrock opens every turn with the same block of system instructions and tool definitions, then appends a conversation transcript that keeps growing turn after turn plus the newest caller utterance. The team enables prompt caching to reduce cost as the session continues. Assume the selected model supports explicit caching and the static prefix meets its minimum token requirement. Where should the explicit cache checkpoint be placed to make the entire static block eligible for reuse while excluding the growing transcript?
options: Immediately after the fixed system instructions and tool definitions, before the growing conversation transcript
At the very beginning of the request, before the system instructions
At the very end of the request, after the newest caller utterance
No checkpoint is needed; Bedrock caches the entire prompt automatically regardless of content
explanation: For explicit caching, placing a checkpoint after the stable instructions and tool definitions clearly marks the prefix the team wants to reuse while later content changes. Eligibility, minimums and TTL still apply, and reads are not guaranteed on every turn. Supported models can also provide implicit caching without checkpoints, and model-specific block lookback may reuse earlier content from a later checkpoint. The selected placement is a clear explicit boundary rather than the only possible caching path.

stem: A Bedrock application is investigating unexpected extra traffic. It wants to alarm on the number of model requests accepted for processing, independently of prompt and response length. It understands that this alone cannot distinguish retries from new requests. Which CloudWatch metric and statistic should it use?
options: Average InputTokenCount.
Sum of Invocations over the alarm period.
Average InvocationLatency.
Sum of OutputTokenCount.
explanation: Invocations counts requests Bedrock accepts for processing, so Sum measures accepted request volume. It excludes throttled requests and requests rejected during input validation before processing. Token counts also depend on payload size, and latency measures time. Confirm actual retries using SDK telemetry or correlated request logs rather than request volume alone.

stem: A summarization team scored a new model release with BERTScore against a set of reference summaries and saw high overlap scores. After release, users reported that many summaries were incoherent and missed the article's main point. What explains the mismatch, and what should the team change about its evaluation approach?
options: BERTScore is deprecated; the team should switch to computing an F1 score against the same references instead

A high BERTScore indicates strong contextual semantic similarity to references, but does not by itself establish coherence or factual faithfulness. Supplement it with calibrated rubric-based evaluation of those dimensions.
The reference summaries were generated by the wrong foundation model, so the team should regenerate them using the model under test
The team should switch entirely to human evaluation for every future weekly release, since it is strictly more accurate
explanation: BERTScore uses contextual BERT embeddings and cosine similarity to measure semantic similarity against reference text; it is not just lexical overlap. That score alone does not establish factual faithfulness, coherence, empathy or brand tone. Choose a rubric-based judge or human review where those dimensions matter, and calibrate the evaluation on representative cases.

stem: A startup just launched a grief-support chatbot. To save time, the team plans to reuse a set of human-graded reference summaries from an unrelated dataset and run automatic reference-based metrics on every nightly build to catch regressions in the chatbot's tone and empathy. What is the flaw in this plan?
options: There is no flaw; automatic reference-based metrics reliably score tone and empathy because they compare against human-graded references

The dataset and metrics do not test empathetic support reliably. Use representative support cases and a calibrated rubric-based judge for routine checks, with appropriate ongoing human safety oversight for this sensitive use case.
The team should switch to Provisioned Throughput to guarantee consistent latency, which will resolve the tone concern
The team should set temperature to 0 so every nightly response matches the reference text exactly
explanation: Reference metrics must match the task and dataset: BERTScore captures contextual semantic similarity, not a complete measure of empathy or safe support behavior. An unrelated summarization dataset is also a poor benchmark. Use a representative support dataset, a calibrated rubric-based judge for routine signals, and appropriate ongoing human safety oversight. Temperature zero can reduce variability on supported models; it does not force a response to match a reference.

stem: A developer is writing internal documentation to help on-call engineers stop confusing ThrottlingException with AccessDeniedException. Which TWO statements belong in that documentation as accurate? (Select 2.)
options: Both exceptions should always be fixed by requesting a service quota increase
ThrottlingException often correlates with peak demand; repeated AccessDeniedException for one new model instead calls for policy, subscription/agreement and model-availability checks.
ThrottlingException means the prompt exceeded the model's context window

For model-specific AccessDeniedException, verify the documented activation prerequisites, Marketplace permissions where required, provider agreement or FTU status, and account/Region availability rather than assuming a universal manual console grant.
AccessDeniedException is always transient and resolves itself after a short backoff delay
explanation: Throttling concerns request/token quotas and calls for bounded backoff plus demand/capacity management. AccessDenied requires inspection of the actual policy and model activation state; many models activate automatically, with Marketplace or provider prerequisites where applicable. Not every AccessDenied is fixed by a console toggle, and pending activation can temporarily delay successful calls.

stem: A regulated application needs to (1) reduce run-to-run variation during model testing where the chosen model supports sampling controls, and (2) retrieve the exact prompt and completion recorded for past supported Bedrock Runtime requests. Which TWO actions address these separate requirements?
options: Pin the model and prompt version and use supported low-variability inference settings, without claiming they guarantee identical output.
Enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 and/or CloudWatch Logs
Enable AWS CloudTrail logging for the Bedrock API
Configure CloudWatch alarms on InvocationLatency and InvocationServerErrors
Increase the model's maximum output token limit
explanation: Supported low-variability settings can make diagnostic comparisons more stable, but cannot guarantee exact regeneration. Protected invocation logging captures supported request and response payloads so an auditor can inspect the original text. Pin versions and record configuration; replay the stored original when exact historical wording is needed.

stem: A team is finalizing its testing and observability standards for a production Amazon Bedrock application. During review, two engineers make competing claims about the platform's built-in capabilities. Which two of the following claims are TECHNICALLY CORRECT? (Choose two.)
options: Lowering supported sampling settings can reduce response variation, but does not guarantee identical completions for repeated inputs.
Tracking only the average value of InvocationLatency is sufficient because it always reflects what slow-tail users experience
A CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationServerErrors metric can trigger an automated notification when server-side error rates rise
AWS CloudTrail records the full prompt and completion text for every InvokeModel call, making Model invocation logging unnecessary
Retrying a failing regression test until it passes is an acceptable way to resolve nondeterministic evaluation failures
explanation: Lower supported sampling settings can reduce variability without ensuring identical responses. CloudWatch alarms can notify on the configured server-error metric. Averages can hide tail latency, CloudTrail is not a full inference-payload archive, and retrying tests until they pass conceals instability.

stem: Which listed evaluation approach compares generated outputs against gold reference outputs using metrics such as contextual-embedding BERTScore or task-appropriate F1?
options: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
Human evaluation
Automatic (reference-based) metrics
AgentCore Observability
explanation: Reference-based BERTScore uses contextual embedding similarity, whereas F1 compares predicted and reference token/label overlap according to the selected task. These metrics require reference data for the stated comparison and are not comprehensive proof of factual faithfulness, coherence or tone.

stem: A RAG evaluation reports low Context relevance, Faithfulness and Correctness. A developer independently inspects the failing cases and confirms the retrieved passages are off topic while the evaluator scores align with expert labels. Which explanation BEST fits this evidence?
options: The foundation model has a hallucination bug that also happens to suppress the context relevance score.
Retrieval is failing to surface on-topic passages, and the poor faithfulness and correctness scores are a downstream consequence of the model having nothing accurate to work with.
The evaluation job's LLM judge is miscalibrated and uniformly under-scores every dimension.
A guardrail's contextual grounding check is silently blocking every response before scoring.
explanation: Here independent inspection confirms an off-topic retrieval result, so retrieval failure is supported by evidence rather than inferred solely from judge scores. Poor retrieved context can contribute to poor answer quality, but low judge-scored metrics alone do not rule out evaluator miscalibration. Verify the retrieved passages and evaluator before assigning a cause.

stem: Two candidate RAG configurations are evaluated with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG evaluation on the same question set. Configuration A: context relevance 0.55, faithfulness 0.94, correctness 0.52. Configuration B: context relevance 0.90, faithfulness 0.91, correctness 0.88. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Configuration A is better because it has the highest faithfulness score.
The two configurations are equivalent because faithfulness is the only score that matters for a RAG system.
Configuration A is better because a model that never adds unsupported content is always safer for production regardless of the other scores.

Configuration B has higher context relevance and correctness with a small decrease in faithfulness, so it is the better balanced option for the stated QA goal; these scores do not establish literal hallucination rates.
explanation: Configuration B has much better Context relevance (0.90 versus 0.55) and Correctness (0.88 versus 0.52), with a small decrease in Faithfulness (0.91 versus 0.94). It is the better balanced listed choice for answering these questions, not superior on every metric. Evaluation scores should not be interpreted as literal probabilities of hallucination.

stem: An application can invoke other Bedrock models, but a new model has an unmet account-level activation or authorization prerequisite. Which exception is consistent with that access failure?
options: ThrottlingException
AccessDeniedException
ValidationException
ServiceUnavailableException
explanation: AccessDeniedException can indicate insufficient authorization or unmet model-specific access prerequisites. Inspect the exact error and model availability/agreement state; current automatic activation does not remove every Marketplace, FTU or account-level requirement. Throttling is a quota/rate issue and ValidationException is an input constraint issue.

stem: A Bedrock application succeeds in one Region but receives AccessDeniedException after failover to another. The IAM role name and application code are unchanged. Which diagnostic action is MOST appropriate before assuming a new manual model-access grant is required?
options: Check the selected model or inference profile, availability in the destination Region, policy resource and condition scopes, and agreement/account-access status using the documented availability checks.
The IAM role's trust policy does not allow assumption from Lambda.
The request exceeds the model's maximum input token limit in us-west-2.
The account has been throttled because of the sudden Region failover.
explanation: A Region failover changes the request context and model resources being authorized. Verify the model is offered in that Region, the selected model or profile ARN is valid there, policies permit the resources, and agreement/account access is satisfied. regionAvailability describes model availability in the Region; it is not evidence that every Region needs a separate manual entitlement grant.

stem: A platform team is building shared error-handling middleware that every internal service will use when calling Amazon Bedrock. For each exception type, the middleware must decide whether to retry automatically or fail fast and alert an on-call engineer. Which design is MOST appropriate?
options: Retry transient throttling with bounded exponential backoff and jitter; inspect and fix invalid inputs and real authorization failures, while handling a verified pending model-activation state with a bounded wait.
Retry all three exception types with the same exponential backoff and jitter policy, since retries are always safe.
Fail fast and alert on all three exception types, since Bedrock errors should never be retried automatically.
Retry ValidationException and AccessDeniedException with backoff, but fail fast on ThrottlingException since it indicates a permanent limit.
explanation: Use bounded backoff with jitter for transient throttling. Inspect input failures and real authorization failures rather than retrying blindly. Current model activation can also have a temporary pending subscription/agreement state, so a bounded wait after verified activation is distinct from retrying a permanent deny. Service/runtime errors need their own documented handling.

stem: An auditor must read the exact completion that a financial-services application returned for a historical Bedrock request. Which approach establishes exact historical replay without assuming a new model invocation will produce identical text?
options: Retrieve and replay the original completion from protected invocation logs or an application response archive, with the associated request, model and configuration metadata.
Increase the maximum token count so responses are never truncated
Enable provisioned throughput to reserve dedicated model capacity
Raise the temperature to reduce the chance of repetitive phrasing
explanation: Exact historical wording should be retrieved from a protected archive of the original response. Re-invoking a generative model is not an exact-replay guarantee, even at temperature zero. Model version and configuration records help traceability; capacity and output-length controls do not establish identical regeneration.

stem: During a code review, a teammate proposes that the prompt-regression test suite wrap each Amazon Bedrock model invocation in a retry loop: if the response does not match the expected golden output, the call is retried up to three times, and the test is marked passed as soon as any attempt matches. What is the MOST significant problem with this approach, and what should the team do instead?
options: Retry-until-pass masks instability. Keep inputs and model settings controlled, reduce sampling where supported, and use repeated-run semantic or structural quality checks instead of treating exact-text equality as guaranteed.
Retries increase cost with no downside to correctness, so the approach is acceptable as-is
The retry loop is fine, but the team should also enable CloudTrail so every retry is recorded for audit purposes
The tests should instead average the token counts across the three attempts to reduce variance
explanation: Lowering temperature where the selected model supports it can reduce sampling variability, but it does not guarantee identical completions. Keep the model version, prompt, inputs and supported inference settings fixed; evaluate repeated runs with appropriate semantic or structural assertions instead of exact-text equality or retry-until-pass. Some models do not accept sampling parameters, so verify the model contract.

stem: A support engineer is trying to reproduce a customer-reported issue by resending the exact prompt that produced an unhelpful Amazon Bedrock response. Each time the engineer resends the identical prompt, the returned completion is slightly different in wording. Which change to the model invocation is MOST likely to make the output reproducible?
options: Use supported low-variability sampling settings while holding the model version, prompt and other inputs fixed; this can make responses more stable but cannot guarantee identical wording.
Increase the maxTokens parameter so the model has more room to complete its response
Enable Model invocation logging so the exact prompt and response are recorded going forward
Switch to a different foundation model that supports a larger context window
explanation: Lowering temperature where the selected model supports it can reduce sampling variability, but it does not guarantee identical completions. Keep the model version, prompt, inputs and supported inference settings fixed; evaluate repeated runs with appropriate semantic or structural assertions instead of exact-text equality or retry-until-pass. Some models do not accept sampling parameters, so verify the model contract.

stem: A QA team compares prompt templates A and B and wants a defensible estimate of their quality difference despite possible model nondeterminism. Which experimental setup is BEST?
options: Use the same representative dataset and pinned model configuration for both templates, apply supported low-variability settings, and compare repeated runs with a fixed scoring rubric.
Evaluate each template on a different randomly sampled dataset and treat the difference in average scores as entirely caused by the template.
Embed a fixed random seed value inside the prompt text so the model treats it as an instruction
Enable a CloudWatch alarm on InvocationLatency for both templates before comparing quality scores
explanation: A fair prompt comparison uses the same representative inputs, model version, supported settings, scoring rubric and repeated trials. Lower sampling may reduce variation but does not eliminate every source of nondeterminism. Comparing different datasets confounds the prompt change; a seed inside prompt text is not an inference control.
